title: Sometime
logline: Finals week: twenty minutes inside somebody else’s argument, one in the morning in a car with no future — and the last night, every place it happened, until the shuttle comes.

previously.text: In a drugstore aisle at half past one in the morning: “Where do you go, Jack?” “I’ll tell you sometime. Not yet.” “Okay.”
Under Theo’s mistletoe Julian kissed her cheek. It was the only time all night you let yourself look, and her eyes came straight to you.
On Del Playa she took your “right now” apart, point by point. “Is it still right now?” … “A no’s a no. For tonight. For that.”
Father Osei: “…a no that is only for tonight has to be said again tomorrow night, and the night after, to a woman who heard you the first time.”
On the beach at Ellery: “Six days.” “You’re counting.” “I don’t count. I have people who count.”
On Gaudete Sunday you went to breakfast instead of Sully’s. At 1:04 the RAZR buzzed on your desk while you slept: *13. —L.*
After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something without moving her lips, and turned it so you could read it: *Better not tell you now.*

highlights.text: On a back porch where you didn’t know anybody, a girl took the cigarette out of your mouth.
On a motel porch above Lucia you told her you’d decided not to be the one who wrecks anything. “Me neither.”
In Eli’s truck you told Becca you’re not right for her. She’d done everything right.
You brought Theo home to Youngstown for Thanksgiving, and your father asked him to say grace.
At a party in Montecito you crossed the room yourself.
In a drugstore aisle she asked where you go. You said sometime.
On her bed on Del Playa you said no, and stayed till it got light.
All of December you stayed away from her. On Gaudete Sunday you missed the Saints for the first time.
At one in the morning, in a car with no future, she said January. You told her to ask you again.
At one in the morning, in a car with no future, you said yes to January.
On the roof, three nights before the longest night, you told her you had something to tell her, and didn’t get to.
On the roof, three nights before the longest night, you got one word into it, and stopped.
On the roof you told her it was the best night you’d had since — and neither of you finished.
On the roof you said you’d say something, but she’d grade it. She said she’d give it an A.
On the roof you didn’t say it. She thanked you.

s01.slug: MONDAY · 12:58 AM · THE LAGOON LAWN, BELOW DELGADO
body: The phone is warm against his ear. The grass has soaked through the seat of his jeans and the shoulders of the Carhartt and gone on soaking, and the voice in his ear is coming up two hours of the 101 from a balcony in Studio City, kept low so it won’t wake her mother.

body.text: Geminids peak at 2. The roof door says alarm will sound. It won’t. Margot’s counting. Bring a coat. —L.

body: He hasn’t answered it. At 12:41 the RAZR went off in his hand in 412, and Skye said, “Are there meteors up there? LA has four stars and they’re all helicopters.” The east stairwell has a window. The lawn has the sky. He took the lawn.

Since then he has been flat on his back below Delgado, reporting. The sky over the Lagoon is black clear to the hills, no moon anywhere in it, and every minute or so something lets go of it and draws a line and is gone. He tells her each one. She casts it.
“Long one. Left to right, over the eucalyptus.”
“Lead,” Skye says. “Give it a trailer.”
“Short one. Barely.”
“Day player. One line. *Sir, your car is ready.* Gone.”

In return she gives him her four, the only lights over Studio City that move, each with a grudge. “That one’s the news. He hovers over the 405 because his wife left him for a traffic reporter. That one’s the police, and he thinks he’s the lead. That one’s a sightseeing tour that took off in 1994 and nobody’s had the heart to land him.” The balcony rail creaks under her. “I don’t know the fourth one. He’s new. He’s got something to prove.”
She wants to know why there are so many tonight. He tells her: the Geminids, the same few nights every December.
“Same night every year?”
“Every year.”
“Then it isn’t a miracle,” Skye says. “It’s a *schedule*. You know how I feel about schedules.”

He does. He lies there with it while a short one goes over, and finds what he wants to say. “The earth drives through what a comet left behind,” he says. “Every December. Same place in the road, on time. It doesn’t have to be a miracle.” A long one goes east to west the length of the Lagoon, and he waits it out. “You still lie down in the cold for it.”

She makes a small sound down the line, put out and pleased at once. “I hate that,” she says. “Point to you. Don’t let it go to your head. It’s a very small point.” The rail creaks again. “Are you lying down?”
“I’m on a lawn.”
“Lie *down*. Flat. I want to hear you lying down.”

He puts his head back on the wet grass and the cold goes through his hair to the scalp, and down the line her breathing changes, listening to him do it — a girl two hours south with all her attention on the sound of him on a lawn — and lying in the cold under all of it with that in his ear is a very good place to be.

Out on the Lagoon something objects in the dark, three times, offended. “What was that?” — “Ducks.” — “Do them.” He does a duck. “That’s a goose with a head cold,” Skye says, and does one back, and hers is better than his, and better than the ducks’. Out on the black water one of them answers her, furious.
Somewhere in the middle of the meteors he tells her about Wednesday: twenty minutes defending somebody else’s argument, in front of the man who assigned it.
“Your Wednesday,” she says. “The promise one.” “That one.” “Bring it Tuesday. I’ll run lines.”

Above him, the roof. He hears it before he sees it, carried out over the lawn by the cold from five floors up: Margot, flat and final, “Thirty-*one*.” Laney shrieks at something. Kevin laughs his laugh. Theo, aggrieved: “That one was mine. I *ordered* that one.” And a voice he would know through a wall — “Margot, that one broke, that’s two, it counts as two” — and along the parapet, against the stars, a row of dark shapes. All but one of them turn back to the sky. One stays at the edge, over the lawn.
At 1:10 a tone cuts into his ear, two notes, and Skye goes on talking under it. He takes the phone away from his head and tilts the screen to his face.
LENA.
“Is that somebody?” Skye says.
The tone comes again. Up on the parapet, the shape that stayed has something small and lit held at the side of its head.

choices.key: On the night of the Geminids Lena called from the roof while you were on the lawn with Skye on the phone. You let it ring out.
response: He puts the phone back to his ear and lets the tone come twice more, and quit. Up on the parapet the small lit square at the side of her head goes dark. The shape doesn’t move from the edge for a while. When he looks again it’s back among the others.
In his ear, about the next one over the Lagoon, Skye says, “Day player,” and that’s all she says about it.

Near the end she yawns down the line and doesn’t bother hiding it. “Go to bed, Ohio,” Skye says. “Count one for me.” She hangs up first. The lawn is cold at once, through the Carhartt, through everything.

choices.text: Look up. Lift a hand to the roof, phone still at your ear.

response: He lifts his free hand off the wet grass, up into the dark, the phone still at his ear. On the parapet the little lit square comes down from the side of her head. Her arm comes up and holds there. She can see him. She can see he’s on the phone.
A second shape comes to the edge beside hers, tall, one hand in a pocket, and stands looking down at the lawn with her until the tone in Jack’s ear gives up.

Near the end she yawns down the line and doesn’t bother hiding it. “Go to bed, Ohio,” Skye says. “Count one for me.” She hangs up first. The lawn is cold at once, through the Carhartt, through everything.

Near the end she yawns down the line and doesn’t bother hiding it. “Go to bed, Ohio,” Skye says. “Count one for me.” She hangs up first. The lawn is cold at once, through the Carhartt, through everything.
At 1:14, still flat on the grass, he does it with his thumb.

response.text: It’s a meteor shower, Jack, not a keg. —L.

response: Up on the parapet nobody is standing at the edge anymore.

s01a.slug: MONDAY · 1:50 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE ROOF
body: At ten to two he goes up anyway. The half-flight at the east end of five; the beige door, EMERGENCY EXIT ONLY · ALARM WILL SOUND, and under it in brown Sharpie *(it won’t)*; the popsicle stick still wedged in the strike plate. It doesn’t sound. Outside there’s the gravel, and the two HVAC boxes humming to themselves, and the parapet, and nobody.

The PHIL 1 final is at eight in the morning; they’ve gone down to bed. The blanket out of Kevin’s Odyssey is folded square on top of the elevator housing, and on it, under a pebble somebody picked out for the job, is an index card in Margot’s capitals.

body: He lies down on the gravel where the blanket must have been. The stones still keep one or two warm places, about the size of people. He lies with the RAZR on his chest while the cold of the roof comes up through the Carhartt into his shoulder blades. It’s the same sky as the lawn’s, with less in the way. He waits. One comes — a long one, low over the hills behind the Grove, slow enough that he has time to sit up for it — and burns down almost to the ridge, and there’s no one up here to say it to.
The phone on his chest says 1:58. Then it says 2:00, the peak, and the sky goes on being very dark and very clear, and nothing else comes.

s02.slug: MONDAY · 7:40 AM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 → THE EVENTS CENTER
body: Gray at the blind, coming up behind the slats from the bottom. Jack has had four and a half hours, and there is roof gravel in the hood of his sweatshirt. Theo is at the mirror in a white shirt with a navy tie around his neck and no knot in it yet. He has an economics final at eight, and he intends to charm it: it can be done, he has explained, if you wear a tie to it and look a little disappointed in the questions.
He starts the knot without turning around. “Forty-four. You’d have liked number thirty. It went the whole way across and Lena said *oh* like it was a person.”

body.text: He pulls the knot up to his collar. “Lena waved at the lawn. The lawn waved back. There wasn’t a dry eye on the roof.” He gets the dimple into the tie on the first try, and goes looking for his other shoe.

body: In the lobby on the way out, the little brass door of 412’s mailbox has something behind its little window: a square red envelope, addressed in block capitals. On the front of the card is a hermit crab in a whelk shell, drawn in ballpoint, with a Santa hat that doesn’t fit him.

Six true facts about hermit crabs are on the back. Number six: they need a friend.

Praying for Nonna.

body: He reads the back, all six, standing at the mailboxes with his backpack half on, and slides the card into the paperback in his back pocket to mark his page.

Finals don’t happen in Sandoval. The registrar puts PHIL 1 on the basketball floor of the Events Center, four hundred folding desks in rows under the championship banners, the scoreboard dark, a smell of floor wax and bad coffee and other people’s fear. Evan Marsh walks the aisles with a stack of spare blue books against his chest and passes the end of Jack’s row twice with his eyes on the far side of the floor. At eight o’clock exactly Hale comes in through the tunnel in the linen jacket, uncaps a marker at a rolling whiteboard on the free-throw line, writes the only question in capitals, caps the marker, and walks back out the way he came.

body.title: PHIL 1 · Final examination
body.text: PROVE TO ME YOU HAVE A SOUL. YOU HAVE THREE HOURS AND I’VE HAD BREAKFAST.

body: Two rows down and four desks over, Lena is in the cardigan with her hair up in a pencil. She reads it and laughs, once, into her sleeve, and comes up out of the sleeve furious with herself, and uncaps her pen. She never turns around.

Jack looks at the question until Evan has come up the aisle and gone again. Then he writes the first true sentence he has — Nonna’s hands on her beads in a bed at St. Elizabeth’s at Thanksgiving, the beads still moving after her eyes had shut — and goes on from there, and doesn’t look up again till the second blue book is full.
At five past eleven he’s on the Events Center steps in the cold sun with a cramp in his writing hand, and the RAZR finds a bar and goes off twice against his hip.

s03.slug: TUESDAY · 11:50 PM · THE SAAB, THE MARINE LAB TURNOUT
body: The top is up. The canvas over them is beaded on the outside with a cold that never quite became rain, and the Saab’s heater runs on the floor like a hair dryer in another room, so that everything below the knee is July and everything above it is December. The dome light is on. His index cards are in her lap.
He said it at the chain, before he had the door all the way open: “Tuesday. No.” “You can’t answer before the question,” Skye said. “It’s in my contract.”

She came up from LA after a fitting — “Ten pins in a skirt I’m not allowed to sit down in. Cassidy goes to Switzerland in January. Wardrobe wants her to look like she’s never been warm in her life, and I’m a tan with a problem” — and Del Playa is full again. “Tomás is back from Baja. He brought Baja with him. There are two guys from Ensenada in sleeping bags in the hall.” She counts it on the steering wheel. “Four surfers and a darkroom. It’s a fraternity with chemicals.” So it’s the car, at the Marine Lab turnout, short of the chain, with the bluff black on one side of them and the sea working at the bottom of it. She’s in the gray knit cap and somebody’s flannel with the cuffs rolled four times, and she has her bare feet up on the dash in the heater’s draft, in December, the braided anklet slid down to the bone. Her shoes are somewhere in the back with the boards she didn’t bring.
“The sleeping way’s closed for the season,” she adds. “There’s a man from Ensenada asleep across my door.”

She wants Hale first. He gives her Hale in pieces: English, fifties, a coal town somewhere underneath the Oxford that comes up through the vowels when he’s angry; silver hair worn too long; a linen jacket with wine on the cuff; reading glasses he loses on top of his own head; a deaf old greyhound called Bishop Berkeley that he talks to like a colleague; a habit of writing to believers on postcards. Five sentences, maybe six.

Skye listens with her eyes on the fogging windshield, and somewhere around the greyhound her chin begins to go up. Her shoulders go back against the seat. By the postcards she has one of his cards held away from her between finger and thumb, like something a student left on her desk, and she’s looking at him down her nose over the top of reading glasses she doesn’t have.
“Mister Costigan,” she says.

It isn’t Hale’s voice. She has never heard Hale’s voice. It’s the voice Jack just described, with the long-suffering chin attached and something under the vowels shoveling coal, and it frightens him a little how much of the man got across the gearshift in six sentences.

She reads the card aloud. “*A promise is made to a person, not to a reason.*” She lets it droop. “How very moving. I have a greyhound who has heard more convincing things than this, Mister Costigan, and he is *deaf*.” She taps the card on the wheel, once, and comes at the sentence with what she always brings to a fight — people. “And if the person goes away?”
For half a breath she’s out of the chin. “You owe me that one since the Starlite,” she says, and puts it back on.
So he goes looking for it, in her car, and it’s at home. Every Sunday his grandmother lights a candle for his grandfather after Mass, and stands there till it catches.

“The person doesn’t go away,” he says. “Not the way you mean. My grandmother lights a candle for my grandfather every Sunday. He can’t hold her to anything. He can’t see her do it. She does it anyway, because she didn’t promise a reason. She promised him. He’s still somebody.”
Hale looks at him over the top of nothing. “Again. You sound like a Hallmark card. Again.”
He says it again, shorter.

“Better. Wrong, but better.” Hale settles deeper into the driver’s seat, the cuff with the wine on it lifted off the wheel. “Your grandmother, Mister Costigan, is a widow in a cold church. She isn’t keeping a promise. She’s keeping *company*. The candle is a habit, and the habit is lonely, and you have mistaken loneliness for fidelity, which is the most Catholic thing I have ever heard.”

“Then she’d light it when she’s lonely,” Jack says. “She lights it Sundays. She lights it when she’s happy. She lit it the Sunday my sister was born. It goes on whether she feels like it or not.” He hears where that’s going, and goes there anyway. “It’s on a schedule.”
Out of the chin entirely, with a finger up at him: “Don’t you *dare* use my schedule against me.” She puts the chin back. “Again.”
He gives it to her again.
“Again. The bishop has nodded off.”
The third time he doesn’t reach for it. It’s there, in his own words, and it’s his, and Hale gives him one short nod, from a great height.
“Your somebody in the seminar,” Skye says, herself again, turning the card over to see whether the name is on the back, “writes a good sentence.” “Hale paired us.”
She gathers the stack off her knee and squares it there, edge by edge, tapping the short sides even, then the long ones.
“You’re not defending the argument,” she says. “You’re defending whoever made it.”
She taps the stack even once more, and holds it out, and he takes it.

choices.text: “It’s the best thing anybody said all semester. I want to do it right.”
response: “Then do it right,” Skye says, and the chin goes back up, and the glasses that aren’t there go back on. “From the top. I’m British.”

She does the deaf greyhound. She lies down across both seats with tremendous dignity, her head on his thigh and her knees against the driver’s door, and lifts one hand beside her head for an ear, cocked toward a sound it cannot hear, and holds it there, mournful, patient, faintly betrayed, until he has to put his forehead on the dashboard. It is the funniest thing he has seen all week, and it goes on longer than it should, and she knows it, and keeps going.

She does. For ten minutes she comes at him with the chin and the cuff and the coal under the Oxford, and finds four new ways into the sentence, and he holds every one. At the end of it she takes the chin down and looks at him across the gearshift.
“You’re going to be fine,” she says. “You’re going to be better than fine, and you’re going to hate it.”

s03a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 12:40 AM · THE SAAB, THE MARINE LAB TURNOUT
body: Some time after midnight the cards end up on the dash, and a little after that they slide off it.

She comes across the gearshift into his lap. The glass is cold against the back of his head and the heater is going at their ankles, and on the way over her hip finds the steering wheel and the horn lets out half a bleat into the dark. She laughs with her mouth in his hair and doesn’t get off him to see whether the Marine Lab heard.

She kisses him the way she argues, quick and then slow, a peppermint from the cupholder still in her mouth. His hands find the hem of her sweater and the warm small of her back under it, and she sits back on his knees long enough to pull the sweater over her head and drop it on the floor with the cards, and comes back down to him in a black bra and the gooseflesh the cold puts on her arms. “The Swedes built this car for exactly this,” she says into his mouth. “They have very long winters.” And it climbs. Her hands in his hair. His mouth on the freckles at her shoulder, the salt there. The windshield is starting to go white at the edges. She’s breathing through her nose against his cheek, fast, and she is laughing a little too, at the car, at the state of the two of them in it. He has Hale’s office at two this afternoon and a priest’s light he could walk past at eight tonight, and neither of them is in this car. She is. Her weight, the heat of her bare stomach through his shirt, her knees tight on either side of his hips, the cold glass at his back the only part of him still in December.
At the height of it her hand goes down his chest to his belt and settles on the buckle, sure of where it is, and stops there.
The clock on the dash says 12:40 in green. It’s Wednesday. By her it’s Tuesday until she goes to sleep.
“Tuesday,” Skye says against his mouth. “Asking.”

She looks down at her wrist in his hand, and then at him, interested, like somebody who has just been shown a new move and wants to see it again.

She laughs into his collar. “Too soon,” she says. “It’s still alive.”

“No.”

s03b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 12:45 AM · THE SAAB, THE MARINE LAB TURNOUT → OCEAN ROAD
body: She doesn’t argue it. She sits back on his knees in the dome light and looks at him, and then down at the top of his jeans, and her mouth goes slowly sideways.
“You said no to *that*,” Skye says. She runs one finger along his waistband from one hip to the other, reading it like a clause she has found a way through. “You didn’t say no to denim.”

Getting his jeans off him in the passenger seat of a 1991 Saab takes both of them and most of a minute. A boot has to go first and won’t. His knee finds the glove box; her elbow finds the horn again, and he reaches up and kills the dome light with his own elbow so the Marine Lab can at least not *see* it, and she is laughing so hard she has to stop and put her forehead on his shoulder. The jeans end up on the dash on top of the cards, one leg hanging down over the radio.

And then it isn’t funny. Her own jeans go faster than his, and the black bra after them, and his undershirt over his head, until there’s nothing on either of them but cotton — his shorts, the white cotton on her hips, the braided anklet cold against his calf — and the windows have gone blind white, and the car is a small warm room with them in it and the dark pressing on the glass. For the first time that’s all there is. The no holds there, at the last of it. He holds it there.

She keeps to it. She keeps to every word. Everything the no didn’t cover she takes, slowly and then not slowly: her mouth on his throat, his jaw, the scar through his eyebrow; her hands everywhere the letter lets them go, which on her reading turns out to be very nearly everywhere; the warm weight of her settling and shifting in his lap. His hands on the long bare line of her back, the dip at the bottom of it, her ribs going in and out under his palms. She’s not in any hurry. She has all of the letter to work with, and she reads it out to the margins.

Wanting her has stopped being a thing he thinks. It’s pressure — behind the ribs, in the hands, at the hinge of the jaw — like the water at the bottom of a deep dive off the dam at Lake Milton, where the farther down you go the harder it leans on you; and there’s no farther down than this, and he keeps going down.

Once a light comes across the fogged glass, white and slow, sweeping right to left, and every bead of water on the inside of the windshield lights up at the same time. A Marine Lab security truck, idling up the service road past the chain, and on, and gone. She laughs with her mouth on his shoulder and doesn’t stop anything, and the laugh goes all through her and into him.

Once, at the top of it, she lifts her head and looks at him in the white dark, and the question is all over her face. She doesn’t say it. She said it already; it’s Tuesday’s, and it’s spent. He shakes his head. She smiles at him like he’s paid her something, and comes back down.

body.text: He knows how near the zipper came. So does she. She never brings it up, and every time her hand goes past his hip he can tell she hasn’t forgotten.

body: Some part of him is already counting what this will sound like said through a screen, and loses count.
Some time after half past one she props her chin on his bare chest and looks at him through her hair.

“That’s twice now,” Skye says. “Twice you’ve said no to me at this car.” She taps his breastbone once for each. “I’m keeping score.” And she puts her mouth back on his, warm, in no hurry, with the windows white and nowhere in the world either of them has to be.

At a quarter past two he walks up from the chain in the dark with his undershirt on backward and the cards in his jacket and the surf loud below the bluff. At the corner of Ocean Road the RAZR comes back on, finds its bar, and shudders twice in his hand.

body.text: Brick 8. Kevin’s asleep on his orgo. Practice? I’ll be Hale. —L.
Never mind. Goodnight. —L.

body: He reads them once, standing on the corner, and shuts the phone. Across the Commons the Brick is dark from the ground up, all but the eighth floor, which is lit from end to end.

Hale’s window is all Pacific this afternoon, white with sun from the sill to the top of the glass, and it lights the room from the sea side only, so that every stack of books on the floor throws a long shadow toward the door. The gold leaf on the pebbled glass has lost another flake off the E since September. Italy is still in the carpet by the desk. The leash is on its hook behind the door, and today there’s a dog to go with it: Bishop Berkeley, gray to the eyebrows, asleep across the one clear avenue to the desk, so that Lena has to step over him in her boots, and does, and he doesn’t stir.

Two chairs have been set side by side in front of the desk and squared to it. Hale is behind it in a dark jacket Jack has never seen, clean at both cuffs, with his reading glasses actually on his nose and not up in his hair. On the blotter in front of him sits a white plastic kitchen timer, the egg-shaped kind that comes free with a set of saucepans.

Lena takes the left-hand chair. She’s in the cardigan over a dark dress and the Justins, her hair down, a capped pen in her folded hands. In the corridor she said *good afternoon* to him, in full, and nothing else. Jack takes the other chair on four hours’ sleep, with the cold of the bluff still in the backs of his hands.

“Miss Broussard first,” Hale says. “Ladies, and the South.” He lifts a sheet of paper off the nearest stack and holds it up to the light. “But before she defends anything, I want this explained. Thursday, two minutes past seven in the morning. No salutation. No argument. No subject line, which in my experience means a student is either in love or in Latin.”

body.title: From: Magdalena Broussard · To: Adrian Hale · Thu 7:02 AM
body.text:
Pondus meum amor meus; eo feror quocumque feror.

—M.T.B.

body: “Translate it, Miss Broussard. For the benefit of Ohio.”

“*My weight is my love*,” Lena says. “*By it I am carried wherever I am carried.* Augustine, the *Confessions*, Book Thirteen.” She uncaps the pen and writes nothing with it. “It’s his sentence, Professor. *A man knows his own heart by what he says yes to.* Mr. Costigan wrote Augustine in October and didn’t know it. I checked his paper. Not one footnote.”

She gives Hale the long way round, because he asked for it and because she has been sitting on it since Thursday. Thomas says the will follows what the mind shows it as good, and Thomas is right, and Thomas is very little help in a hurry. Augustine says a body goes to its own place by its weight — fire up, a stone down, oil to the top of the water — and that love is a weight like that, and a person finds out what theirs is by where it takes them. “His sentence isn’t about choosing,” she says. “It’s about falling. You find out which way you fall by falling.”
Hale turns to Jack. “Is that true, Mr. Costigan? You stole from a bishop?”
“Aquinas would have footnoted him.”
“Aquinas footnoted everybody,” Lena says. “It was how he flirted.”
Hale makes a small noise of pure pleasure and winds the timer to twenty with a crunch. It begins to tick, loud, a cheap tin tick in a room full of books and sea. “Go.”

She stands up to do it. She doesn’t look at her paper once. She takes his October sentence and makes it better than he made it: that a heart isn’t a thing a man inspects, like a tooth, but a thing he finds out about the way he finds out about anybody, by what it does; that Aristotle knew it, that you become brave by doing brave things and only afterward find out you were; that a yes is the one act nobody can do for you, so it’s the one place a man can’t lie about where his weight is. For her example she doesn’t go to Aristotle. She goes to Nazareth: a girl of fourteen or so, told something nobody could have understood, who says *Be it done unto me* and doesn’t know who she is until she has said it. “And then she does, Professor. And so does everybody else, for two thousand years. She didn’t look into her heart and find a yes there. She said yes, and found her heart.” Hale, who has a rule against interrupting the Virgin Mary, waits her out with his fingers steepled under his chin, and then gets in the way.
“Then the drunk knows his heart is a bottle.”
“He knows it’s thirsty,” Lena says. “And he knows it the next day. You don’t learn your heart at two in the morning, Professor. You learn it at breakfast.”
“And the man who says yes to everything?”
“Has a very small heart. And a very busy one.”
Hale tips his chair back, and the chair complains about it, and asks, mildly: “And Mr. Costigan? Does he know his?”

Lena doesn’t look at Jack. She looks at Hale, and keeps her eyes on Hale, and her voice doesn’t change at all. “Ask him where he says yes at two in the morning. I can’t tell you. That’s rather my point.”
“Is that an argument, Miss Broussard, or a subpoena?”
“It’s an argument with a witness.”

response: He looks at her. She doesn’t look back. The pen goes into the pocket of the cardigan, and her hand goes in after it, and she finishes the last four minutes with her hand in her pocket and her eyes on Hale.

When the twenty are up, she has won them, and everybody in the room knows it, including the dog. Hale stops the timer with one finger and turns it back round to twenty without a word about her. “Mr. Costigan,” he says. “Twenty minutes. In her argument, not yours.”
He looks at the greyhound. Berkeley opens one eye at him, with great sympathy, and closes it again.

body: The sun has come a foot along the green carpet while she talked, and Italy is in it now, boot and all, and so is the end of the dog.
Lena sits. Jack doesn’t; he can’t do this sitting down, and Hale, who has stood up to argue in rooms like this one for thirty years, lets him stand.
“You chose the one she didn’t believe, Mr. Costigan.” Hale says it pleasantly, settling back in his chair. “I said I would know. Defend it anyway.”
In her chair Lena turns her face to the window and keeps it there.
“A promise is made to a person,” Jack says, “not to a reason.”

He builds it the way she built it in September, from the bottom up. A reason is a thing a man has; a person is a thing a man is facing. You can’t owe a reason anything, because a reason can’t be let down. Every promise worth the name is made so that it will survive the day its reasons go — *for worse*, *in sickness*, *till death*: the back half of the vows is nothing but a list of reasons going away, and a man saying he’ll stay anyway. He has her paper in his head, her red and his down the margins. Where she argued it like a woman holding a fish at arm’s length, he holds it close, and somewhere around the vows he notices he has stopped performing it. Lena is looking at the sea. Hale gives him six minutes with his chin down on his chest, and then lifts it.

“Hume,” says Hale, “who was right about nearly everything except the French. A promise is a convention. An invention, and a very good one. It’s the clever little tool by which a man ties down his future self so that his neighbor will lend him a horse. The *reason* is the horse.” He sets his fist on the blotter: the horse. “Take the horse away, Mr. Costigan, and what have you got in your hand? A tool. And a tool may be put down. Your vows are the same instrument for the same purpose, with a cow in place of the horse. Civilization is very largely made of tools put down at the right moment. The rest is sentiment and bollocks.”

choices.text: “A tool you can put down. A person you can’t — not without wronging somebody.”
response: “You can put a tool down,” Jack says. “You can’t put a person down. Not without wronging somebody. If I promise you a horse and the reason for the horse goes away, I don’t get to keep the horse. The horse was never the point. You were. I looked at *you* when I said it, not at the horse.”
Hale is pleased, and lifts a finger to show it. “Wronging *whom*, if the reason’s gone? If the man’s gone? Hold that. I’m coming back for it, and you won’t enjoy it.” Jack holds it, and goes on.

response: “My father’s kept a promise to the Cleveland Browns since 1964,” Jack says. “They won it all when he was a kid and they haven’t given him a reason since. Believe me. Every Sunday in the fall he sits down in front of them and gets betrayed, and next Sunday he sits down again. There’s no reason left. There’s a person.”

Hale laughs, a single bark that doesn’t trouble the deaf dog in the least. “The Cleveland Browns as a moral person. Go on — no. Don’t. I can see the season on your face, and I’ve had lunch.” He waves Jack onward with the back of his hand, still grinning, and Jack goes.

choices.text: “Some promises are tools. Give me the ones that aren’t.”
response: “Some promises are tools,” Jack says. “Most of them. I lend you a horse, you lend me a horse. You can have those, Professor. You can have Hume. Give me the ones that aren’t.”

“Generous,” says Hale. “Dangerous. Which ones aren’t?” He waits, with every appearance of enjoying himself, while Jack goes looking, and Jack finds the first one where he left it — the vows, the back half, the reasons going away one by one — and sets it down in front of Hale again, slower.

body: “Before we leave the horse.” Hale still has his finger up. “In November, in my seminar, you argued that the dead are beyond harm. Epicurus: where death is, I am not. Miss Broussard took you apart in front of the room, and I gave her the afternoon.” He lets the finger come down and point. “Have you been converted since? Or are you merely changing sides for the day, like a mercenary?”
“I lost,” Jack says.
“So you did. Then argue like a man who lost, which is to say carefully.”

Hale gets up and goes round the end of the desk, stepping over his own dog, and stands at the window with his back to the sea, so that he’s a dark shape against all that white and Jack has to squint to argue with him.

“Very well. Let me take your person away. Not a fable — it happens on every hospital ward in England on any given Tuesday. A man on his deathbed makes you promise to look after his dog.” He doesn’t glance at the carpet. “You promise. He dies. The dog, being a dog, has no idea any promise was made; the dog would be equally content with the neighbor. To whom is the promise owed now, Mr. Costigan? The man is ash. The animal is indifferent. There is nobody left in the world to wrong.” He spreads his hands against the glass. “Where does your person live?”

He doesn’t wait for it. “And don’t tell me you keep it for *him*. You keep it because you would like to be the sort of man who keeps it. That isn’t fidelity to the dead, Mr. Costigan. It’s a portrait of yourself, hung where the dead man used to be, with a little candle under it so you can see the brushwork.” He lets go of the glass. “Vanity is the only creditor that never dies.”
Jack’s hand closes at his side and opens again. At the window Lena has stopped pretending to look at the sea; she’s looking at the floor in front of her boots, very hard, with her pen in both hands.

choices.text: “To him. The dead are still somebody. The Church is built on it, Professor — so is the law of wills.”
response: “It’s owed to him,” Jack says. “The dead are still somebody. The Church is built on that, Professor — we pray for them, we ask them for things, we don’t stop owing them because they stopped being able to collect. So is the law of wills, and nobody ever accused probate court of sentiment. You don’t tear up a will because the man who wrote it isn’t around to complain.”

“The Church and the probate court,” Hale says. “Strange bedfellows. Accepted — provisionally, the way one accepts a check from a Catholic.” He comes a step off the glass toward Jack, out of the light, so that Jack can see his face again, and it’s having a very good afternoon.

choices.text: “My grandmother lights a candle for my grandfather every Sunday. Nobody’s holding her to it.”
response: “My grandmother lights a candle for my grandfather every Sunday after Mass,” Jack says. “Every Sunday since he died. He can’t hold her to it. My mother would let her off tomorrow, and nobody at that Mass would say a word if she stopped. She does it anyway.”
Hale is quiet against the window for long enough that the sea gets a word in. “Then the promise has outlived its creditor,” he says at last, “and found itself a second one. Who?”
“Her.”

choices.text: “If promises die with people, Professor, Housman owes a lot of refunds.”
response: “If promises die with people, Professor,” Jack says, “Housman owes a lot of refunds. Half of *A Shropshire Lad* is a man keeping faith with somebody who’s been dead since the second stanza.”

Hale gave him that Housman himself, foxed, wartime, for a brother in a cell, and they both know where the punch came from. “Low,” Hale says. “Effective. I’ll allow it.” He looks at Jack a moment longer over folded arms, and then waves him on.

choices.text: “I don’t know who it’s owed to. I know it’s owed.”
response: “I don’t know who it’s owed to,” Jack says. “I’ve been trying to find him since you asked. I know it’s owed.”
“That’s not an argument.”
“No, sir. It’s the thing the argument’s for.”
Hale opens his mouth to make a meal of that, thinks better of it, and moves on.

body: For four minutes more they go at it over open ground, Hale with Hume again and Jack giving him ground an inch at a time and never the inch that matters, until Hale reaches for Williams — his own Williams, Bernard, from memory — and Jack, who has spent three months in that paperback with a pencil, takes it off him.
“Your man in the water,” Jack says. “Williams. Two people drowning, he can save one, one of them’s his wife. And if he stops to work out that it’s permissible to save your wife in cases like this — ”
“— he has had one thought too many,” Hale says, in spite of himself. He has it by heart.
“That’s a promise made to a person,” Jack says. “Not to a reason. Your own guy. Page eighteen. I wrote *yes* next to it, under your *no*.”
Hale stares at him. “Bernard,” he says, “would be appalled to be enlisted by a Catholic.” But he doesn’t say Jack is wrong. Somewhere in there it stops being a game, and Jack couldn’t have said when.
Then Hale stops arguing.

He comes back from the window and sits on the front edge of his desk, close enough to Jack to be rude about it, and folds his arms, and for the first time since two o’clock he isn’t looking at the argument at all. He’s looking at Jack, with the kind of interest he usually saves for a paper he’s about to enjoy failing.
On the carpet Berkeley sighs in his sleep and stretches all four legs at once, as far as they go.

“You’ve been very good for fourteen minutes,” Hale says. “Good is cheap in this room. I want something dearer.” He tips his head toward the window without taking his eyes off Jack. “Do you believe it, Mr. Costigan? Or does she?”
There are a lot of answers in Jack, and all of them are true enough to say in this room, and only one of them has a person in it, and she’s sitting four feet away with her face to the glass.
At the window Lena has gone very still, her capped pen lying across both palms like something she’s been asked to hold for somebody.

response: “I believe it,” Jack says, “because I watched her live it.” He says it to Hale, because Hale asked.

Lena doesn’t move. Hale, on the edge of the desk, unfolds his arms slowly, and puts his hands on his knees, and has, for once, nothing at all ready to say. On the carpet Berkeley’s ribs go up and down.

choices.text: “It doesn’t matter who believes it. It’s true or it isn’t.”

response: “It doesn’t matter who believes it,” Jack says. “It’s true or it isn’t. A promise doesn’t get truer because I mean it, and it doesn’t get falser because she didn’t. You can’t get out of an argument by finding out who said it.”
Hale looks at him, approving and disappointed in the same breath. “Spoken like a Thomist,” he says, and Jack can’t tell which of the two of them it’s aimed at.

response: “You drink alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight,” Jack says, “and say Housman to the window, Professor. I wash your glass. That’s a promise kept after the reason died.”

The room holds it. Hale doesn’t get up off the desk, and he doesn’t look away, and the sea in the window behind him goes on being much too bright. When he speaks it’s in the same mild voice as before, with something underneath the vowels that came up from a long way off.
“That was very nearly cruel, Mr. Costigan,” he says. “Go on.”
Lena turns from the window and looks at Jack. It’s the first time she has looked at him since two o’clock.

“Yes,” says Hale, unsurprised. “And then?”
“And then I couldn’t find the hole in it either.”
At the window Lena’s thumb stops moving on the cap of her pen.

At the window Lena puts her hand over her mouth and leaves it there. Hale regards the pair of them from the edge of his desk. “Everyone in this room works for her, Mr. Costigan,” he says. “Some of us have tenure.”

body: The timer goes off on the blotter behind Hale: a tin rattle that goes on far longer than anything that size should be able to, while Berkeley, who can’t hear it, sleeps through every second. Hale reaches back and smothers it with his palm.
He sits there on the edge of the desk a while longer with his hand on the timer, and looks at Jack.

body.text: “You won,” Hale says. “Don’t do it to anyone you love.”
“You defended it like a man defending a person,” Hale says. “That isn’t philosophy, Mr. Costigan. It may be better. I shan’t say so in writing.”
“That was an argument,” Hale says. “I’m told they still occur.”
“You defended her with jokes,” Hale says, “which is how the English defend everything. You’re from Ohio, so I’ll allow it.”
“Adequate,” Hale says. “Which from me, in December, is a sonnet.”

body: He takes his hand off the timer. “You chose the one she didn’t believe,” he says, “and defended it as if she did. I told you I’d know.” He looks from Jack to the girl at the window and back. “I don’t yet know what I know. Marks post Monday.”
He turns to Lena. “And you, Miss Broussard, will kindly stop sending me Latin before breakfast. At my age it’s bad for the heart.”
“It was Augustine, Professor,” Lena says. “He’s good for the heart.”
“He was very bad for his mother’s.”
Lena gives him that one with a small bow of her head, and gets up, and starts buttoning the cardigan from the bottom.

The Pacific has gone from white to gold in the window while nobody was looking at it. Hale drops the timer into the top drawer of his desk, where it lands on something that clinks, and shuts the drawer with his knee. He gets up then, and takes a long dark overcoat off the hook beside the leash, and shrugs into it, and wakes his dog with the toe of one shoe. Berkeley unfolds himself off the carpet in sections. Hale clips the leash on by feel.
“Go home,” he says, to the both of them, “the pair of you.”

The Williams is in Jack’s back pocket today — *Moral Luck*, Cambridge, 1981, Hale’s pencil and now his own going at Bernard Williams down every margin, two hands thirty years apart. This morning he moved the Benedict holy card into it out of the *Big Sur*, for the occasion. He takes the card out now and puts it in his shirt pocket, and the Pope goes in over his heart with the corner sticking up.

choices.text: Give it back. Margins and all.
response: He holds the Williams out across the desk, margins and all. Hale takes it and riffles it once with his thumb, the pages going by full of two kinds of pencil, and stops somewhere in the middle and reads whatever Jack wrote there, and snorts, and closes it on his finger.
“I’ll read them at Christmas,” he says, and puts it into the inside pocket of the overcoat. “I have nothing else to do.”

choices.text: “Keep it till January? It’s a hostage.”
response: “Can I keep it till January?” Jack says. “It’s a hostage.”

Hale looks at the back pocket where it lives, and at the corner of the Pope sticking up out of the shirt pocket above it. “A man who keeps my books comes back for the next one,” he says. “Take it to Ohio. Argue with it in the snow. Bring it back with more in it.”

choices.text: Leave it on his desk on the way out.
response: On the way to the door he sets the Williams down on the blotter beside the timer, square to the edge, with no speech attached.

Berkeley feels it land through the floor, and lifts his long gray head toward the desk at the end of his leash, and lowers it again. Hale looks at the book, and then at Jack in the doorway, and nods, once.

s05d.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:05 PM · HOLLIS HALL, THE STEPS
body: Outside, the sun is low and cold and very bright on the steps, the kind of December sun in California that lights everything and warms nothing. Somebody’s bike lock is ringing against a rack in the wind. Lena is sitting on the top step with her bag in her lap and the cardigan buttoned to the neck, and when he comes out she moves her bag to make room.

body.text: “We were good,” she says.
“We were *very* good.”
She takes that with a tilt of her head, and the tilt turns into something else, short of a smile, before she puts it away.
“We were good,” she says.
“You were.”
She looks at him sideways. “The booth,” she says. “I didn’t know you could do that.”
“Neither did he.”
She looks out over the Commons, into the wind, and gives him nothing else for it.

body: She stands, and gets her bag up onto her shoulder. “I’m going to Julian’s. It’s his last night — he drives to Oakland in the morning. I said I’d make him dinner.” No apology in it and no explanation either; she promised, so she’s going.
She goes down two steps and stops there, with the cold sun on half her face.
“Laney booked my shuttle,” she says. “Quarter to five Saturday morning. To the airport. She says I’m on yours.”
“Theo booked mine.”

Lena looks up at him from two steps down. He looks back. A gull goes over toward the lagoon, shouting at the wind. Whatever the word is for Laney Price and Theo Vance booking the same van at quarter to five in the morning without telling either of them, it doesn’t get said on the steps of Hollis Hall.
“Quarter to five,” Lena says, and goes on down the rest of them.

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them. Has a deaf old greyhound named Bishop Berkeley. Brought him to the Blessing of the Animals to annoy Fr. Osei. Osei finished his limerick for him. Asked me if the Housman had gone. Says when you leave something, look at it. Newman did. Threw a dinner at the cliff end of Del Playa. Told a man asking Yusuf about Fort Hood that Yusuf’s a guest, not a spokesman. Read our margins out loud. Stopped in the middle of Lena’s, and folded it away. Told Caleb he doesn’t answer devotion. Collected our margins. Read Lena’s on mine: Neither do I. The final’s oral, December 16th — each of us defends the other’s best argument, and he’s the opponent. Told the room to keep Yusuf’s chair. The last seminar: Lena said nothing for an hour, and he told us to note the date. By Friday we each email him which of the other’s arguments we’ll defend. If we pick a weak one, he’ll know. Both picks came in. Not surprised, not disappointed — at his age the same thing as joy. Wednesday, two o’clock. Come as you are. The oral: she’d sent him Augustine. Lena first, then me. He knew which one I’d picked. I don’t yet know what I know, he said.

s06.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE SIDE AISLE
body: By eight the blue panes of St. Brendan’s have gone black, every one of them, and the church is down to two lights: the sanctuary lamp up front in its red glass, steady, and one bulb over the side aisle that somebody has left on for the line. The line is three folding chairs outside the coat closet, KNOCK (GENTLY) on its index card, and one man ahead of him, a stranger with a backpack between his boots, older than a student, elbows on his knees, reading the floor.

In the back pew Gus is asleep sitting up in the ship’s-wheel sweater, a hymnal face-down on his chest and the church’s ring of keys in his fist, waiting to lock up. Through the closet door Father Osei’s voice comes and goes with somebody else’s, a murmur with no words in it.

Through the glass in the side door, past the olive tree and the dead sprinkler, one window of Newman House is lit. The office. The priest it belongs to is on the other side of the closet door, and the lamp is on anyway.

Jack’s knee is going under the folding chair. At ten to one the Saab will be idling somewhere in the dark with the top down; he hasn’t thought it once since Hollis, and his knee has thought it all evening. The man with the backpack looks at the knee. Jack stops it.

The closet door opens on a girl in a Marisol hoodie with her eyes on her shoes, and the stranger knocks and is let in. He’s in there nine minutes by the RAZR’s outer screen. When he comes out he shoulders the backpack and goes out the side door into the courtyard, under the lit window, and the closet door stands open on the kneeler.

choices.key: Wednesday at eight you went into the box.
Wednesday at eight you walked past the light.
response: He goes out the side door the way the stranger did, across the courtyard under the lit window and down to Ocean Road, and when he looks back from the crosswalk the light is still on, and it’s on when he looks back from the Delgado steps.

s06a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:10 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE CONFESSIONAL
body: He knocks, and steps in, and pulls the door to behind him.

The kneeler on this side; the linen screen on its wooden frame, with the violet of a stole showing through; the old coat hooks along the back wall; the Prodigal Son thumbtacked inside the door at the height of a kneeling man’s eyes. On the far side the folding chair gives a little under the priest, and the bad leg goes where it goes.
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned.”
“It’s been four days since my last confession.”
He has the week as a list. The list holds for about a sentence.
“Saturday night she came to where I work. And after, on the wharf —” He doesn’t finish it. The rest is the sentence Osei heard on Saturday afternoon, only later, and colder.
“Another picture. I opened it, and I answered it.”
“I slept at her house. Just slept. I knew I shouldn’t be there.”

body.text: “And Monday I lied to a friend. By text. About finals.”

body: “And last night.” This is the one he walked over carrying. “In her car. It went further than it’s gone.”

body.text: “I said no late. Later than I should have.”

body: “I said it before I got in the car,” Jack says. “Like you told me.”
“And?”
“It held.”
“Then you know it can.”
For a while there’s only the church on the other side of the door: Gus’s pew creaking once, the furnace coming on somewhere under the floor.
“Last night,” Osei says. “Who chose the hour?”
“She did.”
“And the place?”
“She did.”
“And who walked down to the car?”
On the back of the door the Prodigal Son is down among the pigs, at eye level.
“I did.” And because it’s the truth, the rest of it: “She asks every night. She told me it’s on her call sheet.”
“Then she keeps a schedule,” Osei says. “And you keep the appointment.” “You are not avoiding the occasion, my friend. You are scheduling it.”
“It’s held,” Jack says. “Every time. The line’s held.”

“I know. I thank God for it.” A pause. “It is not the line I worry about. It is the man who stands on it every night of the week, who is getting very tired, and who keeps signing up for the late shift.”
“I am not taking back Saturday,” Osei says, gentler. “Every word of it is still true. What is in it is good, and you want her good. I believed you then. I believe you now.”

“So will it. If you will her good, stop meeting her at the edge of what you can’t give her. Every night you walk out to that edge together, and every night you ask her to stand there with you and hear no. In Kumasi a man came to me with the same burn on his hand four nights running. The fourth night I stopped dressing it, and asked him where he kept the stove.”
“When do you go home?”
“Saturday.”

“Three weeks, then, and two thousand miles. Distance is not a virtue. But it is a mercy. Use it.” And, with what sounds like a smile behind the linen: “Let a different priest hear you at Christmas. It will be good for both of us.”

s07.slug: THURSDAY · 12:50 AM · THE SAAB, THE BLUFF ROAD ABOVE ELLERY
body: No moon. It went new before dawn yesterday, and tonight there isn’t a paring of it anywhere. The coast north of campus is as dark as he has ever seen a place with people in it, black from the hills clear down to the water, and out on the water the platforms sit lit in their rows like a town that came loose and floated off. The top is down. The cold comes over the windshield and gets into his collar, and he lets it.
Her college station is playing Tom Petty, low — a song he knows from the radio in his father’s garage, one guitar and a voice in no hurry at all.

She picked him up at the Marine Lab chain at twenty to one with her hair stuffed up under the gray knit cap, and kissed him before he had the door shut, across the gearshift, cold-nosed, with one hand inside his jacket against his ribs to see if he was warm. He wasn’t. She kept the hand there anyway, up Ocean Road and out past the last lights of campus, and drove with the other.

North of the Lagoon there’s nothing on the coast road but the two of them and the dark, and she gives him the tour, bright and bored, nine tours into her day. “On your left, the Pacific Ocean. Please do not touch the Pacific Ocean. On your right, California. Gift shop at the end.” A pair of eyes in the brush at the shoulder, green, and gone. “Local wildlife. Union.” He’s laughing; she hasn’t cracked once. “If you look up, those are stars. They’re real. We had them flown in.”
A quarter mile short of the turnout, where the bluff road tips down toward the sea, Skye reaches over the wheel and switches off the headlights. Then the engine.

The Saab doesn’t mind. It goes on downhill on nothing, rolling, the tires loud on the gravel and the road gone out from under the windshield. There isn’t a road. There’s a darker dark where the road ought to be, and the platforms for a horizon, and over the open car every star he has ever been told about, out all at once, so many the sky looks grainy with them. He has one hand braced on the dash and the other on her knee. She’s laughing, steering by something he can’t see, and Petty keeps on through the speakers like nothing’s happening.
“Skye.”
“I know where it goes.”
“You can’t see where it goes.”
“GM’s deciding if my car gets to live,” she says. “It was on the radio. I wanted to see what it does on its own.”
“You’re out of your mind.”
“I’m from Lancaster,” Skye says. “Out there we do this on purpose. There’s nothing else to do.”

What it does is slow on the flat at the bottom, and take the turnout’s gravel under its tires with a long crunch like a crowd settling, and stop with its nose at the rail and the black Pacific in front of it. She pulls the brake. It ratchets. Jack takes his hand off the dash. His heart is going like he ran here.
At the chain, before he got in, he’d said it: “Whatever happens. No.” “Nothing’s happening,” she said. “I’m *talking* tonight.”

She doesn’t start the engine again. She sits with both hands up on the wheel of a parked car where a driving instructor would want them. She drives with one wrist hung over the top of it, or with a knee; he has never seen her hold it like this.
“Thursday,” Skye says. “Not asking.”
After that she says nothing. She waits, hands on the wheel, for him to turn his head and look at her.

choices.text: “Then I’ll ask something. What are we, Skye?”
response: “Then I’ll ask something,” he says. “What are we, Skye?”
“You stole my scene,” she says, and the corner of her mouth goes up and won’t come back down.

choices.text: “Are you breaking up with me? We’d have to be something first.”
response: “Are you breaking up with me?” he says. “We’d have to be something first.”
“That’s the scene,” Skye says. “Sit still. I wrote it.”
He waits.
She takes a breath like somebody about to go under a wave, and takes her hands off the wheel.

s07a.slug: THURSDAY · 1:05 AM · THE SAAB, THE BLUFF ROAD ABOVE ELLERY
body: Petty runs out. A boy on the college station comes on half asleep to say that was Tom Petty and this is the overnight, and something about a benefit show in Las Olas on Saturday, and Skye reaches over and turns him off. The dark comes in where the radio was. At the foot of the bluff the surf works at the old pier pilings.

She gets the striped blanket out from behind his seat — the beach one, Ellery still in its creases — and shakes it out over the both of them, and turns in the driver’s seat to face him with her back to the door and her knees drawn up under it.
“Here’s my pitch,” she says. “We stay like this.”
“Like this.”
“A few more weeks. The car. One in the morning. You on a lawn doing ducks.” She pulls the blanket to her chin. “Not before Christmas.”
“What happens at Christmas?”

“Everything. That’s what’s wrong with it.” She says it fast, like the setup to something. “Christmas and New Year’s put too much pressure on new things. Everybody’s drunk and somebody’s mother is crying in a kitchen. I’ve watched it happen on four sets and in one kitchen.”
“My mother makes everybody put their phones in the bread basket on Christmas Eve,” he says. “At the door. Like a toll.”

“See?” Skye points at him across the gearshift. “That’s a woman under pressure.” Her thumb finds a loose thread at the blanket’s hem and goes to work on it. “And then you’re in the snow and I’m here, and it’s two thousand miles of phone. Long distance is two people holding phones and pretending it’s a person. I’ve never done it. I don’t want to find out I’m bad at it with you.”
He turns that over in the cold. It sounds like a good reason, and he was raised around good reasons; his mother keeps a drawer of them by the stove.
“We’d be the same two people on the phone either way,” he says. “If we both know, why not now? What’s a word going to break?”

“Oh, Jack.” She comes up off the door. “Everything. A word breaks everything. Listen. Two people are a couple on the twentieth. Great. On the twenty-fourth there’s a second drink, and a cousin — there’s always a cousin — who leans across the table” — she leans across the gearshift and does him, a cousin with a mustache and a beer in his fist — “*so what are you two*, and he says *together* and she says *talking*, and now they’re in a fight about a word with two thousand miles in the middle of it, and neither of them can see the other one’s face, which is the only thing that would’ve fixed it.” A finger up, before he can come in. “On the thirty-first somebody takes a picture at midnight. She’s in it. Some guy’s arm is around her, because it’s midnight and arms go places. It means nothing. It’s on the internet by ten after twelve, and he sees it in a basement with his grandmother asleep upstairs.” She tips her head. “Who wins that fight?”
“Nobody.”
“The cousin,” Skye says. “The cousin always wins.”
“Then we tell the cousin to mind his business.”
“You have never told a cousin to mind his business in your life. You’d pass him the bread.”
He has cousins. He can see exactly which one would lean, and over which bread basket.
“The cousin always wins,” he says.

She settles back against the door, satisfied, and looks up at the stars instead of at him. The thread comes loose from the hem. She winds it around one finger, tight, till the tip goes dark, and lets it off, and winds it again.
“I want to keep this,” she says. “That’s the reason under the reasons. Everything I ever watched get broken got broken between the twentieth and the second.”
“What do you want to keep?”

She thinks about it with the thread. “This. One in the morning. You telling me the earth drives through a comet on schedule. The part where you don’t want anything out of me but the next line.” She winds it tighter. “It’s rare. I’d like it not to go to a party.” She looks over at him. “Whatever it was in December, I’m not asking. January’s mine.”
He looks out at the sea. One of the platforms has a red light on top of it that blinks, and he counts it four times before he can look back at her.
“So,” Skye says. “Go home. Text me from the snow globe. When you get back, we’re dating. Officially.” She lets the thread go. “I’ll make it a whole thing.”
The cold sits on his face. Under the blanket her feet find his leg, cold as the rail, and press there.
“How’d it go? Your twenty minutes.”
“Fine.”

“*Fine*. You’ll have to do better than fine in January.” She sits up into the cold with the blanket around her shoulders like a cape. “Here’s mine, then. I just gave you a lot of reasons. Forget them. Those are for Christmas.” And she says his sentence back to him, word for word: “A promise is made to a person, not to a reason. So I’m not making it to a reason. I’m making it to you.”
Down at the pilings a wave comes in bigger than the others, and the sound of it comes up the bluff a second late.
“And you can not-trust yourself all January,” Skye says. “I’ll be right there.”

response: “Yes,” he says. “I want that.”
She doesn’t have anything ready. Her mouth opens on nothing and shuts again, and her feet go still against his leg.
“Good,” she says. “I was going to do it anyway. I’m glad it’s mutual.”

response: “Do I get a vote?”
Skye looks at him across the gearshift in the starlight, at all of him. “You just voted,” she says. “With your whole face.”

response: “A whole thing?”

She squares her shoulders under the blanket and looks into a camera somewhere over the glove box, and she’s reading the eleven o’clock news. “Tonight, a source close to the couple confirms,” she says, grave as a flood warning, “that it is, in fact, a whole thing. More at eleven.” And then, herself, pulling the blanket back up: “I’ll tell my mother last.”

response: “Ask me again in January.”
She looks at him. She winds the thread back around her finger.
“I’m not going to ask,” Skye says. “In January I’m going to *tell* you.”

s07b.slug: THURSDAY · 1:30 AM · THE SAAB, THE BLUFF ROAD ABOVE ELLERY
body: “I’m not counting, by the way,” she says. “Before you ask.”
He hadn’t been going to ask. She has her arms around her knees under the blanket, and her eyes on the platforms, and her chin down on her wrists.
“I counted,” Skye says. “Twenty-four days. Till you’re back.”
He looks at her. She’s looking at the sea.
“The dorms open the tenth,” she says then, fast. “I get the housing emails. I don’t live in housing. I read them anyway, like a cookbook.”
“What are you doing for it?” he says. “Christmas.”

She gives it to him in order. Her mother’s, by dawn. The network’s party on Christmas Eve, where her mother wears a sweater with a reindeer on it that lights up, and tells everybody Skye is resting. “And a party in the hills on the twenty-second. Everybody I went to middle school with.” She makes a face. “Christmas Day we do a hotel, so nobody has to cook. There’s a brunch. My mother tips the omelet man like he’s family. He sort of is.” She pulls the blanket tighter. “You?”
“Snow. Three days of my grandmother’s bread. Midnight Mass at St. Brigid’s, and my father asleep on his feet for the homily.”
“On his *feet*?”
“It’s a gift. It skipped me.”
“In January,” Skye says, “my publicist’s going to want lunch. Wear the blazer from the rain.”
“And I’m keeping your shirt over Christmas,” she says. “The blue one. You said you wanted it back.” “I said I wanted you in it.” “Both,” Skye says. “That’s what January’s for.”

Around half past one the cold wins. She gets up on her knees on the seat and hauls the top forward over them by its frame, and it comes down out of the stars and latches at the windshield, one side and then the other, and the sky is gone. It’s the canvas a foot over their heads, and the blanket, and the smell of her hair.

She comes back across the seat to him the way she always does — and then, on purpose, he can see it’s on purpose, she doesn’t. She stops with her mouth just off his, and waits. It’s Thursday. She isn’t asking.
So he does what she taught him. He says it.
“I want you,” Jack says. “I’ve wanted you since the chain.” His hand is at the hem of her sweater. “I want to see you.”
She laughs, very low, and lifts her arms over her head.

So it’s his hands. The sweater, over her head, and the knit cap with it, so that her hair comes down full of static and crackles against the canvas. The flannel under that, a button at a time, slow, because he wants it slow. The rest of it, her jeans and the clasp at her back, which his fingers have never done — every time before tonight she’s been the one — and his fingers are stupid with it in the cold, and she lies back against the door with her arms up on the cold leather and watches him be stupid and doesn’t help, and when it gives she says, very softly, “There he is.”

After that there’s nothing on her but the white cotton at her hips and the braided anklet, and his own shirt and the undershirt under it are on the floor where he threw them, and in the dark under the canvas there are his hands, and it’s his doing, all of it. She doesn’t steer. She lies under his hands and lets him find out what he does when nobody is making the case for him, and what he does is go farther than he ever has: his mouth down the middle of her, the St. Michael medal swinging off his own chest onto her stomach so that her breath goes in sharp at the cold of it; her hands in his hair, holding on; her heel hooked behind his knee. He says her name into her skin and she arches up off the seat to meet it. His hand is at her hip. His thumb is under the edge of the last cotton she has on, and the edge is right there under his thumb, and there is nobody in this car to stop him but him.

response: “No,” he says — to himself — and takes his thumb out from under the cotton, and puts the hand flat on her hip above it, and holds it there.
She hears it. She lies still under him, breathing.
“I didn’t ask,” she says.
“I know.”

response: “Skye.” His hand stops where it is. “I want to. No.”
She pulls his head up by the hair until his mouth is on hers. “I didn’t ask,” she says against it.
“I know.”

choices.key: On the bluff she didn’t ask, and you were the one who went too far. You stopped yourself, and told her exactly how close you came.
response: He takes his hand back, and tells her. Exactly how close. It doesn’t take long to say, and he says all of it, with his forehead down against her collarbone where he doesn’t have to see her face.
She’s quiet. Then she lifts his face in both hands and puts her mouth on his. “I know,” she says against it. “I was there.”

response: He takes the minute. It’s his — not hers, not the car’s, not the hour’s — and he knows it while he’s taking it, every second of it, with his thumb where it is and her breath coming short against his ear.
Then: “No.”
“I didn’t ask,” Skye says.
“I know.”

s07c.slug: THURSDAY · 1:50 AM · THE SAAB, THE BLUFF ROAD ABOVE ELLERY → THE TURNOUT CHAIN
body: And it doesn’t stop. She pulls him back down by the neck and keeps him there, and the no stays where he put it and everything this side of it goes on — nothing comes off, nothing goes back on. His hand stays on the right side of the line he drew, and every minute it knows exactly where the line is, and every minute he has to put it there again himself.

body.text: The minute he took is in the car with them. She doesn’t mention it. He can feel her not mentioning it every time she moves.

body: It’s the slowest it has ever been, and the longest. She takes her time and so does he. Her skin is cold wherever the air gets at it and hot everywhere else; her mouth tastes of the cold; her hands go down his back and stay low and hold on. Their breath goes up the inside of the windshield and takes the platforms out of it one at a time, till the last light at sea is a smear on the glass and then there isn’t any, only the dark and her. Once the seat lever gives under his knee and the seatback drops flat with both of them on it, and she laughs up at the canvas, helpless, and pulls him back down by the ears. The clock on the dash goes past two. He doesn’t look at it again.
“Jack Costigan,” she says once, low, into his mouth.

At twenty past two she lifts her head and squints at the green numbers and says a word that would get her sent out of Sister Rose’s fifth grade. “Studio City by six,” she says, “or my mother calls the Highway Patrol. She’s done it before.”

They dress by feel in the dark. She finds his undershirt wedged down the side of the seat and he finds her sock on the gearshift, and they put themselves back together in the cold without much talk. When he’s done she turns on the dome light and looks him over, frowning, and fixes him: turns his collar right side out, does the top button, pulls his jacket zipper up to his chin and stands the collar up at the back of his neck with both hands.
“Wardrobe,” she says.
She puts her forehead against his for a minute under the dome light, and turns it off.

She drives him back down the coast with the headlights on this time and stops short of the Marine Lab chain at 2:35. He gets out. She leans across the seat after him, the gray cap back on crooked, her hair still full of static.
“Merry Christmas, Ohio.”
She puts it in gear, and the Saab goes off down the service road toward the highway and south, one taillight a little dimmer than the other.

At the chain the RAZR comes back on and finds its bar and shows him 2:37, and nothing else. He puts it in his pocket. His collar is still done up to the top the way she left it, and it’s cold enough out here that he leaves it that way.

s08.slug: THURSDAY · 8:35 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: The sun is just up over the hills, low enough to come straight through the Fishbowl’s glass and lay itself across the carpet in long panes, and none of it is warm. Jack has the armchair nearest the window and the last of the lobby urn in a paper cup, burnt, with a lid he has been biting. He’s had four hours. The glass is doubled and lets nothing in from outside but the light: the front circle, the palms, the bike rack, without a sound.

In the circle, with its engine running, there is an old tan Volvo wagon with a dent in the tailgate, loaded to the roof for the drive north — a duffel, a laundry bag, a box of records — and across the back seat, belted in like a passenger, a guitar case.

Julian is standing at the open driver’s door in a gray cardigan with his keys in his hand. The lobby doors open, and Lena comes down the front walk in her coat with her arms already folded against the cold, and he meets her halfway around the hood. He takes her face in both his hands and kisses her, on the mouth, unhurried, in the low sun, with the Volvo idling beside them, and her hands come up and hold on to his wrists.

The cold comes off the glass onto Jack’s knuckles. He has the cup in both hands. Through the double pane it’s perfectly quiet — no engine, no gulls, nothing of theirs, only the exhaust going up white past the palms and her hands still up — and the lid gives under his thumb until coffee comes up through the slot and runs over his fingers, hot, and he leaves it there. He watches it to the end. It is daylight, and she is twenty feet away on the other side of a window, and none of it is his to look away from.

Theo comes down the east stairs at twenty to nine in the camel coat over pajama trousers, carrying an espresso from the machine in 412 in a white demitasse, saucer and all. He reaches the Fishbowl’s doorway as Julian comes in through the lobby, and lifts the little cup to him. “Drive safe, Julian,” he says sweetly. “Or don’t. Either’s fine.”
“Morning, Theo,” Julian says, in the same voice he’d use for anybody, and comes on across the carpet to Jack with the cold still on his cardigan.

He holds out his hand, and Jack has to put the coffee on the windowsill to take it. Julian’s grip is warm and dry and calloused at the fingertips, and he holds on while he talks. “I’m off. Oakland by two, if the 101 behaves, and my mother’s car.” He looks at Jack. “She says you’re on the same van Saturday.”
“Quarter to five.”

“Make sure she eats before the flight. She won’t. She’ll say airports don’t count. Then she’ll have forty minutes in Phoenix and spend every one of them on the phone with her mother.” He lets go of Jack’s hand. “If she starts humming low, under everything else, like a pedal tone, that’s hungry. Feed her.”

journal.title: Julian Park-Ellis
journal.text: Julian Park-Ellis. The guitar guy from the Lighthouse stairs. Plays Bastille Thursdays. Wrote a song called “Fresno.” Plays it once a month. All Souls: came to St. Brendan’s to write Nora Calloway’s name in the book. She was his friend. They sang together. He saw us leave in the second chorus. Something new Thursday. A handshake you’d trust with anything. Sunday he came to the nine o’clock with Lena. Didn’t receive. Had the Sanctus by ear by the end. Picked Lena up at twenty to twelve for the vampires, straight from Bastille. Friday he brought her juk in his mother’s thermos and asked her what she’d go to jail for, and listened to all of it. Drove down from Oakland for the nine o’clock; his brother Daniel’s home from the Navy. Two coffees on the wall. Asked me to stay to the end of the new one. Thursday at Bastille: it’s called ‘Magdalena.’ It’s good. The Advent party: plays piano too, by ear. Under contraband mistletoe he kissed her cheek. Kissed her goodbye at his car, for Oakland. Asked me to make sure she eats before her flight.

response: “I will.”

“Thank you,” Julian says. He says it to Jack’s face, the way he’d thank a man for holding a door in the rain, and it seems to be what he came in for. He pats his pockets once for his keys, finds them in his hand, and goes.

The Volvo goes around the circle and out onto Ocean Road with the guitar case riding in the back. Lena stands on the curb with her arms crossed against the cold until it’s gone, and a little while after, and then comes in past the Fishbowl with her eyes on the stairs.
“She’ll eat if it’s beignets.”
“There are no beignets at the Santa Barbara airport.”
“There’s a Cinnabon in Phoenix.”
Julian smiles at the carpet. “Then you know her,” he says, and lifts a hand to Theo in the doorway on his way out, and Theo, after some thought, lifts the demitasse.

“I will.” Julian smiles a little, at the difference between this one and the one he got at the door, and nods to Jack, and goes.

s09.slug: THURSDAY · 9:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: “Happy Birthday” goes around the Fishbowl in five keys. Kevin takes the bottom of it like the choir man he turns out to be; Laney takes the top in a key of her own; Doug comes in a bar late and stays a bar late out of loyalty; Theo doesn’t sing at all but conducts, with a plastic fork. Lena finds an alto line under Laney and holds it there. Jack has the melody, mostly to himself. At the head of the coffee table, behind the candles, with her arms folded, Margot endures it to the last *you*.

Margot turns nineteen on Monday, the twenty-first: the solstice, the longest night of the year. She has described it in Jack’s hearing as a personal brand. By Monday everybody will be gone, so Laney has done it tonight, early, against the birthday girl’s stated wishes, with a grocery-store sheet cake and black frosting that took her twenty minutes at the Vons bakery counter. “The lady said black is for Halloween and the Raiders,” Laney says. “I said, ma’am, she is *both*.”
