body.text:
HAPPY SOLSTICE MARGOT
(EARLY)
(UNDER PROTEST)

body: The candles are a wax 1 and a wax 9. “They had a six,” Laney says, “but Priya’s here.”

“I heard that,” says Priya, who has come down from 401 in a fleece with her keys on a lanyard and accepted one slice, on a napkin, standing. She looks at the cake. “Fire code permits one candle per cake. That’s two.” She takes a bite. “I’m choosing joy.”

There is Martinelli’s in Dixie cups, because the only person in the room old enough for anything stronger is Priya, and she’s on duty. Margot blows the candles out in one breath and the presents come across the table to her.

Theo’s is two paperbacks soft with age, wrapped in a page of the *Financial Times*: *Le Deuxième Sexe*, Gallimard, 1949, both volumes. Margot opens the first and looks at the title page for some time, and then up at him. “This is a first edition.”
“It was in a box.”
“Whose box?”
“A box’s.”

Kevin’s is a brass jingle bell on a red ribbon. “For your door,” he says. “Every door should have one. Clinically.” Doug leans across and jingles it next to his ear, delighted — “*Duuuude*” — and Kevin takes it out of his hand and gives it back to Margot, and his eyes come across the room to Jack, once, and go back to the cake.
Lena’s is a dozen pralines from home in wax paper, packed in a Café du Monde can with the coffee long gone out of it. “The South owes you an apology,” she says.
“For which part?”
“Start with the pralines and work up.”

Yusuf has brought news instead. Margot accepts it in lieu. “Tariq comes home the twenty-third. We have fourteen stairs. He’s done eleven.” He lifts his Dixie cup. “My mother is buying a fifth rail.” Kevin drinks to that before anybody, and then all of them do.
Then Margot stands up, which at a party is not a thing she does.

“I want to say something on the record,” she says. “Once. It will not be repeated, discussed, quoted in my column or brought up at my funeral, Delaney. In September I would have described you as a sample. Two Catholics who argue for sport. A third who sings bass. A Texan. A man from Bakersfield. An engineer from Fremont. A resident advisor. And Theo.”
“Thank you,” says Theo.
“You are the strangest people I know. I grew up in Portland. I know a woman who keeps bees in her hair.” She looks down into her cup. “I like you.”
A small silence goes around the Fishbowl, and Doug, who has a piece of cake halfway to his mouth, holds it there.
“Strike that,” Margot says. “Unsourced.” She stands a moment longer with the cup in her hand and leaves it in, and sits down.
Lena turns to Theo while Laney is cutting the corners off for whoever wants corners. “What are you doing for Christmas, Theo?”
“LA,” Theo says. “A lot of parties in the hills.”

“Logistics, y’all.” Laney is licking black frosting off the cake knife. “Theo’s driving me to SBA at one tomorrow, and then he’s going to go see the blue people in IMAX. Kevin’s taking Yusuf home at half past three. Margot’s shuttle’s at four. Lena’s flight’s Saturday at six twenty-five, Jack’s is seven-ten, the van’s at quarter to five, Theo booked Jack’s, I booked Lena’s, it’s cheaper for two.” She sets the knife down on the cardboard. “So Friday night it’s just y’all.”
“And Priya,” says Margot.
Kevin, to the frosting: “Leave it alone.”
“Leave *what* alone, Kevin, I’m reading a *schedule*.”
Lena looks from one of them to the other with her eyes narrowed. Theo is cutting himself a second piece of cake along a ruler only he can see, and is very interested in it.

They stay. Doug falls asleep upright on the end of the couch with the bell in his lap, where Margot has let him keep it. Priya goes back to 401 and comes down again for a second slice, standing. At ten past twelve Margot looks up at the clock over the Fishbowl door, once, and then across at Jack, in the armchair by the glass where he has been since the singing, and goes back to her cake.
Laney holds up her Dixie cup. “Fireman. Toast. You’re the only one who hasn’t.”

journal.title: Yusuf (PHIL 9H)
journal.text: Fremont. Engineer. Fasting for Ramadan through a ninety-minute seminar and funnier than all of us. Broke the fast with his people on Mission Street and fed me till I couldn’t stand. Father on the NUMMI line since ’85. Brother Tariq interprets for the Army in Helmand and calls on Sundays. The day of Fort Hood I asked if Tariq was okay. He’s not in Texas. Friday morning he called: he’s fine, and he said don’t watch the news. Yusuf watched the news. At Hale’s table a man asked him what Muslims think. He’d like one week where nobody asks. His nineteenth, at Bastille, with a candle in a scone. He watched the memorial Tuesday. Standing up. I didn’t ask. The night of the West Point speech: ‘You left the first time. My father watched you leave. If you’re going to come, stay.’ His brother Tariq — an IED in Helmand. Alive. Germany. I went after him. We sat on the east stairs. Back for finals the night before Oslo. Tariq’s learning stairs. He’d like the speech to be right. Tariq home the twenty-third. Fourteen stairs; he’s done eleven. A fifth rail.

body: By noon the last exam block has let out, and everybody on the south side of campus who can get outdoors has. The sun is out over the Commons, low and white, and the lawn is still wet where the Brick’s shadow lies across it. People stand around on the grass with their blue books rolled up in their fists and their suitcases parked beside them by the handle, and up on somebody’s shoulders by the library steps a boy in a Santa hat is waiting with a ruler for a baton.

At twelve the Ferrer Tower gets through the Westminster quarters, off-key, and then the first notes of “Hotel California” come down out of the louvers one bell at a time, slow and lopsided: a rock song played on a hundred and thirty feet of concrete by somebody in oven mitts. The flat bell is in it. It falls on the end of every chorus, a hair under true, and every time it does the lawn cheers it like a field goal and the boy in the Santa hat brings the ruler down.

Theo is on the path in the camel coat with Laney’s pink carry-on at his feet, holding it by the handle at arm’s length, as if it might go off. Laney mouths every word with her eyes shut and her sunglasses pushed up into her hair. Margot, beside her in black with her arms folded, is not singing; on the chorus her mouth moves anyway, and stops whenever Laney’s eyes open. Kevin has the Odyssey keys on one finger and spins them on the beat. Yusuf has his last blue book under his arm and winces, on principle, at every flat note. Down by the path to the Lagoon, Priya holds a clipboard of checkouts against her chest and ticks somebody off it in time.

Lena isn’t far off, at the front of a knot of girls from the second floor, in the cardigan with a scarf wound twice around her throat. Through the second verse she has her face tipped up to the top of the tower — to the louvers, where the two of them stood in October at five in the morning, her on the high bells and him on the low. Her eyes come down off it, across the grass, and find him. She doesn’t smile. The chorus comes round, and when the flat bell lands on the end of it she hums the note along with it, low, and he’s near enough to hear that she has it exactly as flat as the bell. She goes back to the tower.

The bells can’t manage the last line, the one about checking out and never leaving, so at the end a few hundred people on the grass sing it for them, badly, and applaud the tower, and the tower goes back to being a clock.

journal.title: The Ferrer Tower
journal.text: A hundred and sixty steps. VIVOS VOCO · MORTUOS PLANGO · FULGURA FRANGO, around the biggest bell. I call the living, I mourn the dead, I break the lightning. One bell is flat. She says it isn’t. Thursday the fifteenth, at five in the morning, we played the Saints on it. Half of Anacapa turned its lights on. Nobody knows who. Margot’s following up for the *Tide*, from a minivan: the police log says one of them was laughing; the bass came in late twice. Nobody confessed. The last day of finals, at noon: ‘Hotel California,’ the flat bell and all. She hummed it.

body: Theo’s half of 412 went to Los Angeles yesterday by FedEx: three boxes and a garment trunk. (“I don’t carry, Costigan. I *forward*.”) What’s left on his side is what was never going: the TV, the espresso machine, Rosie’s two princes taped up over the desk, the garment bag over the back of the chair, and Nonna’s twenty, folded small in the frame of his mirror. He stops at the espresso machine. The Post-it on its flank has been there since Labor Day, gone soft at the corners, and over the fall it has grown a line at a time in Theo’s neat hand. The last line is in fresher ink.

+ 1 MALIBU —T.V.

+ 1 LIBRARY (12:30)

body: “Malibu,” Theo says, reading down it like the specials. “Labor Day. A classic. The hold — my finest hour with a bursar. Jack has woken up to that square of yellow from his pillow every morning since September.
Theo peels it off the machine and holds it up at shoulder height, a waiter presenting the check.
“I never leave a ledger open over the holidays,” he says. “Ledgers get ideas.”

choices.key: Theo held up the tab. You let him tear it up.
response: Jack doesn’t reach for it.

Theo waits to see whether he will. When he doesn’t, Theo tears the Post-it in half along the line under MALIBU, and in half again, slowly, and lets the quarters go into the wastebasket under the desk one at a time, as solemnly as earth onto a coffin.
“Merry Christmas,” he says. “Don’t be weird about it.”
On the foot of Jack’s bed, folded in a square, is the gray cashmere throw off Theo’s own bed. “For Ohio,” Theo says. “I’ve been. It’s cold.”
On his way to the door he slides Nonna’s twenty out of the frame of his mirror, folds it once more along its old crease, and puts it in his wallet. “For LA.”

Down in the front circle the SL is idling with the top up, the garment bag laid along the shelf behind the seats and Laney’s hatbox strapped onto the trunk rack. Laney is in the passenger seat in her sunglasses, with her two suitcases packed into the footwell around her shins. s10b.slug: FRIDAY · 2:30 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE MARIAN SHRINE
body: In the middle of a Friday afternoon St. Brendan’s smells of cold wax and the lemon oil Mrs. Fitch works into the pews before Christmas, and the blue glass puts the side aisle under water.

Jack has crossed Ocean Road with a dollar in his hand to light a candle for Nonna before the flight, and somebody has beaten him to the shrine. At the votive rack under Our Lady, with her oxblood Doc Martens planted on the tile and a long match going, Margot is lighting a candle in the back row. She gets it on the first try, shakes the match out, and sees him.
“For research,” she says.
He hasn’t said anything.
“If you tell Lena,” Margot says, “I’ll tell her you cried at Sully’s in October.”
“I didn’t cry at Sully’s.”
“She’ll believe me.” She tips her head at the iron offering box. “The sign says a dollar. I put in two. I won’t be accused of freeloading on the supernatural.”

He feeds his dollar into the slot of the iron box and lights one in the front row for Nonna, off the flame of a stranger’s. Margot hasn’t gone. She stands with the dead match in her fingers and her eyes on her own candle, as though it might be about to do something.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Nineteen on the solstice, four days early, under protest. Likes us. On the record. Lit a candle for research.

choices.text: Kneel beside her and say nothing.

s10c.slug: FRIDAY · 3:25 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE BIKE RACK → THE EAST STAIRWELL
body: By twenty-five past three the sun is low over the Grove and comes in flat under the eucalyptus, and the rack behind Delgado is down to one bike. La Flaca has it to herself: the rust, the wire basket, the seat that tips back when you sit on it, and Ray Ochoa’s clip-on light still on her bars.
Jack unlocks her and walks her round to the front, where Rafi is sitting on the steps with a duffel for his abuela’s between his feet and his skateboard across his knees.
“Boss.”
“Till Christmas,” Jack says, and holds out the handlebars. “It’s Christmas.”
Rafi looks at the bike, and at the light on it, and keeps his hands on his board. “Keep her,” he says. “My abuela says after Christmas a bike decides.”
“Decides what?”
“No stress. She’ll let you know.” He stands, swings the duffel onto his back, drops the board on the walk and pushes off toward the harbor, one foot and then coasting.

At the curb the Odyssey has its hatch up, and Kevin is fitting Yusuf’s bag in beside a case of water and a first-aid kit the size of a carry-on. On the back glass, in La Vang car-wash polish gone a little streaky in the sun, in Lena’s capitals: WHO DAT · 13–0. Kevin brings the hatch down and comes round the van and shakes Jack’s hand, and holds on to it.
“Respectfully, Jack,” he says. “Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something.”
He lets go before Jack can ask him what, and gets in. From the passenger seat Yusuf lifts a hand. “Fourteen stairs.”
“Fourteen stairs,” Jack says.
At half past three exactly the Odyssey leaves the circle at the speed limit and not a mile over.

He walks La Flaca back round and chains her up in her slot. At 3:41 he’s on the landing between three and four in the east stairwell, where the bar is, and the building is quiet enough that he can hear a shower running somewhere far up, and the RAZR goes off in his hand.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Asked the one question I couldn’t answer. Thursday at one in the morning, on the darkest night of the year, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something.

body: At twenty past five the lights in the fourth-floor hall come on by themselves, on their timer, down a corridor of shut doors. Priya has been along it since noon with a clipboard, trying every knob, and on her own door, 401, at eye level, there’s a new laminate.

LAST ONE OUT:
THE LIGHTS ARE NOT DECORATIVE.
— Priya, RA

body: Theo’s half of 412 is down to the bare mattress, a square of cleaner carpet where the minifridge stood, and the espresso machine, unplugged, with its cord wound tight around its middle. On Jack’s bed, folded in thirds at the foot where Theo left it, is the gray cashmere throw. For Ohio.
His duffel is packed and zipped on the floor by the bed, with the Café du Monde can in the top of it, wrapped in his Mooney T-shirt so it won’t dent between here and Glenwood Avenue.

Out the window the Lagoon has gone the last dark blue before black, and the lamps are on along the bike path with no bikes on it. Down the hall the vending machine by the east stairs hums, and clunks, and thinks better of it. Everybody Jack knows is on a freeway or in the air or in a kitchen two thousand miles away, and he is on his bed in his socks with a paperback open on his chest that he hasn’t turned a page of in twenty minutes, and the RAZR shut on the blanket by his knee.
Somebody knocks. Not Priya’s knock, which is three and a clipboard. Two, and then nothing.
He opens the door on Lena in her coat, with two paper cups from the urn at the front desk, the lids on, the last of it. She holds one out to him so she’ll have a hand free.
Something round and heavy pulls the right pocket of her coat out of shape.

When her free hand comes out of the other pocket, an index card comes with it: ruled, numbered, in her capitals, a pen-mark at the left of each line where a box would go. She reads the top of it once, in his doorway, and he gets the first of it upside down before she puts it back.

body.title: An index card, in capitals
body.text:
1. DELGADO — DOWNSTAIRS
2. ST. BRENDAN’S
…

body: “You’re here,” she says.
“I’m here.”
He has been gone every night this month she might have knocked, and he knows it, and here he is in his own doorway in his socks with her coffee in his hand.
“I’ve knocked on this door three times this month.” She looks past him at the stripped mattress, the throw, the duffel. “Tonight somebody answered.”
Jack holds the coffee. It’s too hot to drink and he holds it anyway.
“Everybody’s gone,” he says.
“Everybody but us.”
“And Priya.”
“And Priya.” She takes the lid off her cup to let it cool, and blows across it, and looks at him over it. “Walk me to the shuttle, Costigan. The long way.”
“The shuttle’s at quarter to five.”
“In the morning. I know when it is.”
“That’s eleven hours.”
“Eleven and a half.” She puts the lid back on. “I did the arithmetic.” Her eyes go past him to the foot of his bed. “Is that cashmere?”
“Theo. For Ohio. He says he’s been.”

“He left you cashmere.” She looks at it folded in its thirds on the cheap Delgado blanket, gray on brown. “That’s a love letter, Jack. In Theo.” She steps back into the hall to give him room. “Get your coat.”
On the blanket the RAZR is lying where he left it, shut, with its one bar.

response: He picks it up and opens it and holds the red button down where she can watch him do it. The RAZR plays its little falling chime, four notes going downstairs, and the screen empties.
“I want the whole night,” he says.

Lena watches the phone into his pocket. Then she reaches past him into 412, takes the Carhartt off the back of the door, and holds it out to him by the collar, the way his mother does at the back door on Glenwood in February.

Lena hears it. She drinks her coffee and studies Theo’s espresso machine, wound up in its own cord, until he has his boots on.

response: He switches it off and sets it on the empty desk, square to the edge, where the Dell used to be. “If anybody needs me,” he says, “they can write.”
“Nobody writes, Costigan.”
“Then nobody needs me.”
Lena looks at the little black phone on the bare desk. Then she gets the Carhartt off the back of the door and throws it at him.

s11a.slug: FRIDAY · 5:45 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE BASEMENT → THE 4TH-FLOOR LOUNGE
s11a.music: Lena at the upright — “Walking to New Orleans”
body: The dryers are cold for once. Without them the basement is the boiler ticking somewhere behind the cinderblock and the long tube light over the folding table, buzzing to itself. Priya’s CLEAN THE LINT TRAP is still taped over the machines. Somebody has left one gray sock on top of a washer, folded, as if it might be called for.
Item one on the card is the upright against the far wall, the one nobody in Delgado admits to playing, with its dead F and its cigarette burn on the lid from some decade before Priya.

Lena puts her coffee on top of it, on a ring somebody else left there, and her coat on the nearest dryer. She doesn’t say anything about it. She sits down on the bench and pushes the cardigan sleeves up to the elbow, one and then the other, and lifts the lid.

It’s New Orleans from the first bar. Her left hand starts walking, a slow easy rolling walk with a little hitch in it, and her right comes in over it, lazy and exactly on time. The dead F comes up in the bass every other bar, and every time it comes up she steps around it the way you’d step around a pothole on a street you grew up on, without looking down and without slowing.
She sings the first verse low, under the piano, not loud enough to carry past the folding table — *I’m walking to New Orleans* — and then she stops singing and lets the piano have the rest of it.

Jack sits on the dryer beside her coat with the coffee going cold in his hands. He watches her right foot on the pedal, the scuffed toe of the Justin. He watches the back of her neck where her hair is pushed over one shoulder. She plays it through, every verse, with her eyes on the keys and nowhere else, and she plays it properly — no joke in it, nothing thrown away — and on the last chord she holds both hands down until the basement has it, and then lifts them off.
“That wasn’t Debussy,” Jack says.
“Debussy never walked anywhere in his life.”
She takes her coat off the dryer and her coffee off the piano and goes up the east stairs ahead of him to four.

The lounge is dark. The couches are shapes, the TV is off and looks wrong off, and the microwave clock says 6:12. Lena finds the switch over the counter. Margot’s whiteboard comes up under the fluorescents in layers, a semester of it, nothing ever quite erased: USEFUL IDIOTS FOR CHRISTIAN NATIONALISM across the top with COSTIGAN | BROUSSARD and the tallies under it; LEIF ERIKSON DAY (OBSERVED) gone gray at the edges; AMERICAN GOTHIC (UNPLANNED); a pink pitchfork with a bow on it; UNEXPLAINED CITRUS — FLOORS 2–4, SUSPECTS: (THE CATHOLICS); and down the side Laney’s TIGER column, which says MORE.

body.text: And new at the bottom, in Margot’s capitals, copied off the back of her own hand: TO THE PATRIARCHY — WE’LL ALWAYS HAVE DECEMBER.

body: Lena uncaps the black marker from its string and writes, in a clear corner under Margot’s heading, in capitals of her own: MARGOT: FEELINGS DETECTED.
“For January,” she says. “She’ll erase it. She’ll know who.”
Jack takes the marker. He writes HALE’S ORAL and stops with the cap in his teeth. “What’s the score?”
“He didn’t give one.”
“So we do.”
“Then I won mine,” Lena says. “Everybody in the room knew it. The dog knew it.”
“The dog’s deaf.”
“He slept through yours. He slept through mine *attentively*.”

body.text: “I want a point for the counterexample.” “You get a point for the counterexample. You don’t get a point for the booth.”

body: They go back and forth about it for about a minute, her twenty against his, Augustine against the promise, which one Hale smiled at with both sides of his mouth and which one with only the left, and in the end Jack writes it the only way either of them will sign: HALE’S ORAL — B 1 · C 1 · BERKELEY 1.

The window over the couches is black, the Lagoon gone out behind it, and in it the lounge comes back at them: the dead TV, the board, two people in coats under the fluorescents with a marker and a cold coffee each. Lena takes the card out of her pocket and a pen out of her coat and draws a line through the first line.

journal.title: The whiteboard
journal.text: Margot’s, by annexation: USEFUL IDIOTS FOR CHRISTIAN NATIONALISM, COSTIGAN | BROUSSARD. Sully’s made the board: liturgical football, idolatry, my outfit. Margot wasn’t even there when I read it. She didn’t need to be. Now the chastity talk is up there too: both of us, voluntarily. Kenzie Rourke got her own line. Margot thinks she might not be an idiot. Category pending. C 6, B 5. The morning after the wake, under the total: TUESDAY — NO SCORE. (BEREAVEMENT.) October 9th, top of the board: LEIF ERIKSON DAY (OBSERVED). Columbus: see attached. Then: FERRER TOWER · THU 5:00 A.M. · “WHEN THE SAINTS GO MARCHING IN.” Suspects: a Catholic; a different Catholic. Laney added the Holy Ghost. Margot wrote it up for the Tide and didn’t name anybody. Halloween: AMERICAN GOTHIC (UNPLANNED). Both. C 7, B 6. Somebody drew a pitchfork. Sunday after St. Nicholas: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS — FLOORS 2–4. SUSPECTS: (THE CATHOLICS). Laney’s TIGER column has given up counting. It says MORE. The last night Lena added a line for Margot to find in January: MARGOT: FEELINGS DETECTED.

s12.slug: FRIDAY · 7:15 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S → THE NEWMAN HOUSE STEPS
body: St. Brendan’s is dark but for the red lamp by the tabernacle and the shrine. Without the lights on, the hull of the ceiling is gone up into the black, and the blue glass is black too, and what’s left of the church is the little rack of votives under the Lady, burning low in their red cups, and the brass plate under them catching it.
In the top row one candle has burned most of the way down since half past two.

body.text: Beside it, a little taller, is the one Jack lit for his brother.

body: “Margot lit that,” Jack says, low. “For research. You didn’t hear it from me.”
Lena looks at the candle with real respect. “Of course she did.”

She takes a long match from the box, lights it off Margot’s, and lights one more in the bottom row, under the plate — NORA GRACE CALLOWAY · 1989–2009 — and shakes the match out and kneels. Jack kneels at the end of the rail. He gives the Lady his grandmother and his mother and his father’s truck on the road to Pittsburgh tomorrow night, and a van at quarter to five, and doesn’t get further than that, and she crosses herself beside him and gets up, and he does.
At the door she wets her fingers in the font and crosses herself, and then flicks what’s left on her fingertips at him, for the road. It gets him in the eye.

They go out by the side door into the courtyard, past the olive tree and the broken sprinkler, to the Newman House steps. Father Osei’s Advent sheet is taped inside the glass of the front door at eye level, in his careful hand.

body.title: Taped inside the Newman House door
body.text:
THE O ANTIPHONS · DEC. 17–23 · VESPERS
17 · O Sapientia
18 · O Adonai
19 · O Radix Jesse
20 · O Clavis David
21 · O Oriens
22 · O Rex Gentium
23 · O Emmanuel
— G.O.

body: Lena reads them off in Latin, all seven, in her Rosary pronunciation, the nuns’ vowels, and taps the glass at the bottom. “Now read the first letters. Backwards. From the twenty-third up.”
Jack does it with his finger on the glass. E. R. O. C. R. A. S.
“Ero cras,” he says.
“Translate, Latin Club.”
“*Ero* — I will be. *Cras*. Tomorrow.” He looks at it. “Tomorrow I will be.”

“Tomorrow, I will be there.” She is very pleased with it, and with him. “Some medieval monk hid it in there, upside down at the end of Advent, so that on the last night it answers you. Or that’s the story. Sister Agnes told it to us in the eighth grade like it was gossip.”
Jack laughs out on the step in the cold, and runs his finger up the column again, letter by letter, to watch it work. “He hid a promise in the calendar,” he says, “and didn’t sign it.”
“He didn’t have to sign it,” Lena says. “It isn’t his.”
She taps the second line. “Tonight’s is Adonai. The bush that burned and didn’t burn up.” The third. “Tomorrow’s the root of Jesse.”
“Tomorrow I’m in Denver.”
“Tomorrow I’m in Phoenix,” she says, “eating a pretzel in a terminal and saying Vespers into it. Jesse won’t mind. He was a farmer.”
“You say Vespers in airports?”
“I say Vespers in Laney’s car with the windows down and Laney doing the responses. An airport’s a cathedral.”

The door opens on them. Father Osei is in a brown cardigan over his clerical shirt with a mug of something in his hand, and the light from the hall behind him, and by the look of him he has seen two people in his church after dark through his office window and come out to see which two.
“Ah,” he says. “The last two.”
“We were reading your door, Father.”
“Ero cras,” Jack says.
Osei looks from the sheet to Lena, delighted. “She told you. Good. Most priests don’t know it.” He lowers his voice. “Don’t tell them. They will put it in a homily.”
He sets the mug down on the rail. “You are both traveling tomorrow.”
“Both of us,” Lena says.

Osei looks at the two of them on his steps in the cold, her with her collar up and him with his hands jammed in the Carhartt, and not a hat on either of them. “In Kumasi we would call this weather a reason to stay indoors,” he says. “Here you call it December and go walking in it. Then stand there.” He comes out onto the landing beside them, the bad leg last, and raises his hand.

“Be for them, Lord, a help when they set out,” Father Osei says, “and a comfort on the road. A shade in the heat. A cover in the rain and in the cold. A staff where the way is slippery, and a harbor if they are shipwrecked. And may almighty God bless you, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”
He makes the cross over the two of them, one sign for both, and lets his hand down.
“Come back,” he says.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday, behind the screen: love wills the good of the other — and that’s why it’s dangerous. Gaudete: rejoice is a command. Wednesday, behind the screen: I’m not avoiding the occasion, I’m scheduling it. Distance is a mercy; use it. Blessed us both for the road on the Newman steps. Come back.

choices.text: Ask him to bless your grandmother too.
response: “My grandmother too, Father,” Jack says. “She’s not going anywhere. She’s eighty-four. She’d want to be asked.”
“Carmela,” Osei says. He has had her name since the fall. He turns a little on the step, toward the east, toward Ohio, and makes a smaller cross in the air in that direction. “Done.”
He picks up his mug and leaves them the steps.
“Does it cover airlines?”
“It covers everything,” Osei says, “but the food.” He picks up his mug. “For the food you will need a bishop.”
He leaves them the steps.
“Amen,” Jack says.

Lena says it with him, half a syllable behind, so that it comes out of the two of them with a small echo in it. Osei hears it, and picks up his mug, and goes back up to his door with the leg taking the steps one at a time, and leaves the light on over the steps behind him.

s13.slug: FRIDAY · 8:40 PM · THE 11 BUS → MISSION STREET, BASTILLE (DARK)
body: The 11 into town is nearly empty on the last Friday of the semester and the heater is going full blast for whoever it can get. Lena has the fares in the box, two sets of quarters, before Jack has his wallet out of his back pocket. There’s the driver, with a Santa hat on top of the regular hat, and a man at the back with a Christmas tree in its netting across two seats, holding it by the trunk so it won’t roll on the turns, and them. The bus smells like the tree. Mission Street goes by in strings of colored lights, the Walgreens, the post office, the Mission up on its rise with one lamp on over the doors, and somewhere past the Mission Lena turns around in her seat and asks the man whether it’s for him. “For my daughter,” he says. “She told me get the ugliest one they got.” Lena looks it over through the netting, the bald side and the bent top, with professional seriousness. “You did real good,” she says, and he is so pleased he gets off at the post office still smiling, and thanks the driver, and then, on the way past, the two of them, Merry Christmas.

They get off at the bottom of the grade. Café Bastille is dark for the break. The string lights over the door are off. Inside, through the glass, the chairs are up on the tables with their legs in the air, and the sign-up board by the register where the open-mic names go has been wiped down to a gray smear, except for one line in somebody’s marker across the bottom: BACK JAN 14 · MERRY XMAS · TIP YOUR BARISTA.
They stop outside without either of them deciding to.

Lena stands with her hands in her coat pockets and looks in at the little stage, the stool on it, the mic stand with no mic. “Julian’s going to record it in January,” she says. “In Oakland. His mother found a cellist.”

A week ago Thursday there was a man on that stool singing her name, and Jack in the singer’s empty chair at her table, hearing every word of it. A car goes by behind them, slowly, looking for parking that isn’t needed anymore.
“He’s coming for New Year’s,” Lena says to the dark window. “Mémère wants to hear him play.”

“Daddy’s making him a gumbo. Julian’s never had a real one. He thinks the thing they make in Oakland with the sausage is a gumbo.” She says it fondly, and to the glass, and doesn’t take any of it back.

Jack can see it without having seen any of it: a front room in New Orleans with the good lamps on, an old woman in the best chair, Julian at somebody’s piano being kind about the tuning, and everybody in the room liking him, because there is nothing about him not to like.
Before he can answer: “You never answered me. About staying.” He doesn’t have to. She isn’t waiting for it.

response: “It’s a good song,” Jack says.
“It is.”
She looks in at the stage through the glass, the stool and the empty stand, and then she turns away from it, and they go on down Mission Street toward the water.

choices.text: “Tell the cellist not to leave in the second chorus.”
response: “Tell the cellist,” Jack says, “not to leave in the second chorus.”
Lena laughs, surprised into it, and it comes out of her in a cloud in the cold and goes up past the dark awning. “Walk,” she says, and he does, and so does she.

He doesn’t say anything. He starts walking, and after a few steps she falls in beside him, and they go down Mission Street together, down the grade to the harbor, with the lights of the wharf coming up at the bottom of it.

body: Her quarter goes into the jukebox before she has her coat off. She knows the number without reading the cards. Irma Thomas comes out of the speaker over the pie case, slow and patient, a New Orleans girl in 1963 with a piano under her, and Lena stands there with her coat half off one shoulder until the first line is sung and then comes and sits on the stool next to his.

From the customer side of the counter the Anchor is a different restaurant. Jack has never sat on this side of it with her. The pie case is lit up at eye level, the Hobart is somebody else’s problem, and Rudy at the flat-top lifts his chin at the two of them over a burger and goes back to it, and the ballgame on his radio is a basketball game from somewhere with the volume down.

Gloria comes out of the walk-in backward, pushing the door with her hip, with a flat of eggs held against the other one. She sees who’s on her stools. She sets the eggs down by the grill, and wipes her hands on her apron, and without either of them ordering anything a plate comes down the counter with a slice of pecan on it and two forks crossed beside it.
“Ma’am, I didn’t order this,” Lena says.
“Eat it while it’s warm,” says Gloria, already going back down to the register. “It’s been waiting.”

Rudy comes down from the flat-top a minute later with a basket of fries they didn’t order either and sets it by the pie. He looks at Lena. “The Mission,” he says. “You sang.” “Badly,” Lena says. Rudy thinks about it. “My mother says for the Virgin, loud is the same as good.” And goes back to the grill.
“You don’t order the pecan,” Jack says. “It comes to see if you’re here.”

She picks up a fork. Gloria’s pecan is the dark kind, more pecans than filling, with a crust somebody has been making the same way for thirty years, and Lena takes the first bite with her eyes closed and opens them slowly. “All right,” she says. “All right. That’s a pecan pie.”

She asks after Danny. Jack gives her the last of it: Ma read him the latest one off the envelope on the phone. Danny went to the prison library to look up Flannery O’Connor. His review, in full: she raised peacocks, she was mean, and he likes her.
“Your brother has taste,” Lena says. She points her fork at him. “Tell him I said so. And tell him Merry Christmas from me. With the accent.”
“I don’t do the accent.”
“Then practice.”
She goes back to the restroom past the pay phone. Gloria stops at the register across from him, ringing up nothing, and says it low, with her back half to him.
“That one’s still standing in it, hon.”
In the glass of the pie case his own face is laid over the lemon meringue. He looks at it until the restroom door opens.

Lena comes back and takes the second-to-last bite of the pecan without asking and announces, to Jack and the pie case and Rudy, that the Saints are going to beat Dallas tomorrow night, because it’s ordained.
“God doesn’t care who wins football games,” Jack says.

“He does so.” She sets the fork down to have both hands. “Providence goes all the way down. Every sparrow. Every hair. Thomas says it extends to singular things, not just the species — you don’t get to have a God who runs the universe and can’t be bothered with a field goal. And the Saints aren’t a football team. After the storm the whole city was a FEMA trailer. Daddy has had the same two seats since 1981, and the night they opened the Dome again he sat in them, in a building they’d scraped the storm out of, with seventy thousand people on their feet, praying. That’s a liturgy. That’s a city’s petition.”

“Thomas also says secondary causes,” Jack says. “God doesn’t kick the ball. He moves the kicker by letting the kicker kick. He cares about Hartley — his soul, his mother, his hamstrings. Not the score. The score is the kicker’s job.”
“You don’t get to use Thomas on me. Thomas is mine.” She picks up the fork again and points it at him. “Then why do you pray before the field goal, Costigan?”
“I don’t.”
“Washington. Overtime. Before the snap. At the top of your lungs.”
“That was the Who Dat.”

“The Who Dat,” Lena says, “is a question addressed to the heavens. *Who dat say dey gonna beat dem Saints?* It’s practically the Book of Job.” She takes the last bite. “Fourteen and oh tomorrow night. It’s ordained.”

journal.title: Gloria (the Anchor)
journal.text: Hired me for rating her pie a four. Rated me a lattice-top. I’m not going to ask. Told her I won’t be the next guy at the door. She says nobody holds a door that long without somebody else walking through it. Asked after the pecan. I said she’s seeing somebody, he’s nice. She said lattice-top. Boxed a pie for Nonna. From a woman who’s been on her feet thirty years. Peach is August. St. Nicholas Eve, at the end of my shift, low, at the pass: ‘Pecan came to see if you were here.’ Gave my Thursday to Hector — his girl’s due at Christmas. ‘Don’t argue with a baby.’ Says I look like the pie case at closing. Rated somebody new. Boysenberry. ‘That one’s not waiting for any door.’ The last night: two forks and the pecan, at the counter. ‘That one’s still standing in it, hon.’

response: “Then Providence owes Detroit an apology,” Jack says.

“Detroit has *Dale*,” Lena says. “That’s Providence. Dale is a sign and a wonder.” She isn’t giving him an inch of it, and they go two more rounds on it — the Lions, Job again, whether a man in a Barry Sanders jersey at ten in the morning counts as a mortification — before she lets him have the last word by eating his.

At a quarter to twelve Gloria lays the check face down at Lena’s elbow and takes the pie plate with the two forks on it. The pecan isn’t on the check. Lena turns it over, and reads it, and turns it back, and puts down a tip that would embarrass both of them if either said anything about it.

choices.text: “Fine. He cares. He’s a Saints fan.”
response: “Fine,” Jack says. “He cares. He’s a Saints fan.”
“Everybody is,” Lena says, “eventually.” She clinks her coffee cup against his, satisfied, and holds it there against the rim of his before she drinks.

“Out loud?”

Lena puts her hand down flat on the Formica between their cups as if he’d signed something, and leaves it there while Irma Thomas finishes.

s13b.slug: SATURDAY · 12:05 AM · THE BEACH, WEST OF THE HARBOR
body: They take the beach home. It’s three miles west from the harbor to the bluffs under Las Olas, and the tide is out far enough to give them the hard sand, packed and ribbed and shining a little where the water has just left it, and the night has gone very cold and very clear. The stars come down to the sea. Offshore the oil platforms are lit up, each one its own small town, and behind them the wharf and the Anchor’s sign get smaller every time Jack looks back, until he stops looking back. It smells of kelp and cold salt. Their breath goes ahead of them. They don’t talk much. She has the card in her pocket and he can hear her thumb going along the edge of it.

The wind comes straight off the Pacific into their faces with nothing in its way since Japan. Lena puts her chin down into her collar against it. “Three miles,” she says into the collar. “About.” “Good,” she says, and a few hundred yards past the breakwater, without a word about it, her arm comes through his and holds on. One. Her hand stays in her own coat pocket with his elbow clamped against her side, so that he has to shorten his stride to hers and she has to lengthen hers to his, and after a hundred yards or so they have it worked out. They walk west like that on the hard sand with the surf breaking white on their left, toward the dark end of the beach and the wooden stairs up to Seacliff Road.

s14.slug: SATURDAY · 12:50 AM · SEACLIFF ROAD, THE LIGHTHOUSE BACK PORCH
body: The porch light still works. They come up the bluff stairs at the dead end of Seacliff and around the side of the last house, past a recycling bin full of Pacifico bottles and a surfboard rack with no surfboards on it, and at the foot of the back steps the motion sensor finds them and the deck jumps out of the dark: the gray boards, the hot tub under its blue tarp, the chili-pepper lights along the rail unplugged for the break with half the peppers still dead. Taped inside the slider, in marker, a paper sign: GONE TILL JAN 11 · DON’T EVEN.

Past the rail the ice plant runs out to the chain-link fence and the gap where the post rotted, and past the fence the Point is a black shoulder against more stars than August ever let anybody see out here. No fog tonight. It’s very cold and very clear, and the old light on top of the Point is only a shape.

Lena goes up the steps first and gets up on the rail with her back to the post, boots crossed at the ankle, and waits for him to work out that he’s supposed to stand where he stood. He stands there. She nods at the dark slider, at a living room with one couch and a lava lamp in it, unplugged. “Pastel polo,” she says. “By the fridge.”
“Sigma Rho legacy,” Jack says. “Two DUIs.”
“He ran for Congress. He won.” She settles her shoulders against the post. “We threw him a parade. The FBI is looking into the parade.”

They do the Jell-O girl and the boy she was spoon-feeding (“Engaged,” Lena says. “June. Lime at the reception.”) and the Nietzsche man on the couch (“Still recurring.”), and then they’ve run out of people who were here, and she looks at him from the rail with the porch light white on her face. “Go on. What did you actually think.”

“I thought, that’s the pelican girl.” He leans his forearms on the rail beside her boots. “I’d watched you beat a parking cop that morning with a lamp in your arms. I thought, she’s going to be a problem for somebody.”
“For somebody.”
“I didn’t know yet it was a whole floor.”

“I thought you’d come out to be sick,” Lena says. “I had the hydrangea line ready. I’d already used it on two boys from Sigma Rho. You were the first one who said anything back.” She looks at the slider, where the party was. “And then you said *jagoff*.”
“Technical term.”

“Remy says it now. At LSU. You have a fraternity in Baton Rouge saying it wrong.” She pats the pocket of her coat, where the tin is. “And number one. Right here. You lit it off a Bic like a man in a war movie.”
“You took it out of my mouth.”
“Those’ll kill you.”
“That’s the plan,” he says. “Slowly.”
“Like a Catholic,” she says with him, and they both hear how bad it is, and say it anyway.
“You want to know where Sad Irish Poem came from?”
She sits up on the rail. “Laney won’t tell me what you said. I asked her on her mother’s pearls.”
“The living room. Before the Jell-O. She grabbed me by the chain around my neck and said I looked like a sad Irish poem, and I said, ‘I’m not sad. I’m Irish. It’s a different thing.’”
Lena stares at him. “That’s it?”
“That’s it.”
“She has called you a poem for four months on one line.”
“She called you a coward on less. I carried that one out here myself, with her lipstick on my face.”

“And I let you sit there an hour with it,” Lena says, and that’s the end of her. She laughs until she has to grab the rail with both hands to stay on it, boots knocking the post, and he laughs because she is, and the porch light shakes on the boards with the two of them.
When she can talk she points at his eyebrow. “And the Ukrainians.”
“The Ukrainians did it.”
“Pierogi aren’t even Italian.”
“That’s what made it a tragedy.”
“I still don’t believe a word of it.”
“It’s oral tradition.”

“It’s lying. It was lying then.” They argue about who won the porch. She was on the rail first, so it was hers; he says that’s squatting. He got her name first, so it was his. “You got my name off Laney,” she says. “Laney yelled it at Hawaii. That isn’t getting. That’s weather.”
“Then Laney won.”
“Laney always wins. It’s the first thing you learn.”

Then they’ve been still too long. The porch light clicks off, and the house gives up on them. The dark drops over the deck, and then the stars come up through it over the Point, more of them every second his eyes give back to him. Either of them could wave an arm and bring the light back.

“You were very hard to find this month, Jack,” she says, looking out at the Point. She says it the way she’d say it was cold, a thing about December, and he waits for her to set it on the rail and leave it there.

She doesn’t, quite. “You’ve never just not answered me,” she says. “Not once since August. Not when you were mad at me. Not at three in the morning when I was being ridiculous. You always answered. Even if it was only to tell me I was being ridiculous.” Her boots uncross and cross the other way. “I offered to be Hale. I’d have been a *good* Hale.”

body.text: “And when you did answer, it was *can’t, finals*.” She lets one breath go up white in the dark. “To a meteor shower.”

body: “And you’ve never missed a Saints game at Sully’s. Not one. Every game since September you were in that booth in black and gold, praying for field goals you swear you don’t pray for.” She says it to the Point. “Sunday I texted you the number. You were supposed to be sitting right there when it happened. I didn’t have anybody to turn around to.”

Then, to him: “And you used to come to me. Whatever was going on. Your daddy. Nonna. Me being impossible. Something went wrong and you came and found me, and sat there not telling me what it was until I made you. That was the thing about you.” Her voice doesn’t go up or down. “Now something’s wrong, and you stay away. You talk to me when you can’t get out of it. Across Hale’s carpet. Over Margot’s cake.”
“Something’s hurting you,” Lena says. “Bad. I can see that much from here.”

And then she stops. He watches her do it: her mouth closes on whatever was next, and her hands go back into her coat pockets and stay there, and her eyes go back out to the dark shoulder of the Point and the old light on it. She doesn’t ask him what. She doesn’t ask him who, or where. She sits on the rail of the porch where they met with her hands in her pockets, and waits, and doesn’t make him.
He has a sentence. He has had it since a drugstore aisle, and it’s right there now, in the dark, with nothing in the way of it but him.

choices.key: On the Lighthouse porch Lena named the month — the texts, Sully’s, the staying away. You started to tell her where you go. You got as far as “sometime.”
response: “You asked me where I go.”
“I remember,” Lena says, in the dark.

He gets as far as the next word, and the next word is a person, and the only way to say who is to say why it matters that he says it to her, on this rail, tonight. He has it standing in his mouth, and he can’t.
“Sometime,” he says.

There’s only the sea at the foot of the bluff for a while. “You keep saying that,” Lena says, “like it’s a day of the week.” She doesn’t pick it back up. Her boot finds the post and taps it, twice, and stops.

choices.key: On the Lighthouse porch Lena named the month — the texts, Sully’s, the staying away. You told her you were sorry, and not why.
response: “I know,” he says. “I’m sorry, Lena.”
It isn’t the why. They both hear that it isn’t. It’s what he has.

“I know you are,” Lena says. “I wasn’t collecting.” She takes one hand out of her pocket long enough to point at his eyebrow. “Sorry doesn’t get you out of the Ukrainians, though.” “Nothing gets me out of the Ukrainians.” “No,” she says. “Nothing does.”

response: He keeps it. She watches him not say it; in the dark he can feel her do it, every second of it. Then one hand comes out of her pocket and finds the rail beside her and holds on, and she looks back out at the Point, and after a minute she starts telling him what she thought of his shoes that night, which was nothing good.
