response: “I’d like to file a complaint,” he says, “about the night we met.”

She could leave it lying there. She doesn’t; she picks up what he’s handing her, and he hears her do it. “Overruled,” Lena says. “It was a *great* night.” In the dark he hears her settle back against the post, and then she says it again, quieter. “It was.” And a minute later: “You told me the postcard was classified.” “It was.” “It still is,” she says, and he can hear she’s smiling.

s15.slug: SATURDAY · 1:50 AM · THE POINT PATH → THE WALL
body: The sea is louder at the fence. Lena gets there first — she slid off the rail without a word, took the card out of her coat and held it up to the stars as if she could read it by them, and put it back with nothing crossed off — and at the gap where the post rotted she says, “I’ve got a letter to answer. Out there,” and goes through it without slowing down.

He has watched her stop at this house all semester. She said she was cold. She said it to Laney, too. He goes through after her. Out here the sea is at the foot of the bluff on their left the whole way, seventy feet down, working at the rocks in the dark, and the path runs pale along the lip of it through the ice plant with the wind coming straight off the water into their faces. She walks ahead of him with her hands in her coat and her head down, fast.

Once, where the path dips, she stumbles and catches herself without putting a hand out, and keeps going. The old light comes up ahead of them, squat and white and locked, a county sign on the door warning about the cliffs and no lamp in it since 1967. Past it, the low stone wall: knee-high on their side, and on the other side nothing at all. And at the wall a white wooden cross, her name burned into the crossbar, with a bunch of supermarket roses in a rubber band leaning against the foot of it, most of a week old, gone soft and dark at the edges.

Lena stops at the cross and stands looking at it with her hands in her coat. Then she crouches and takes the roses out of their lean and knocks the dead leaves off the stems against her boot and stands them back up against the foot of it, straighter, the rubber band turned so it doesn’t show. She crosses herself, quickly, the way you’d do it passing a church in a car.
“Somebody leaves flowers every Sunday,” she says, standing up. “Nobody knows who.”

She takes off one glove to get the envelope out of her coat. It’s a plain white one with a Christmas stamp, the flap tucked in, gone soft from being carried. “It came to the Newman office. From Selma. Father Osei gave it to me Sunday, after the Gaudete Mass.” She holds it a minute. “Her mother. Rosa. It’s the first Christmas. She says she’s going to write every one.”
“Nora was my host,” she says. “You know that.”
He knows that.
“It was my weekend. The Saturday.”
The end of April; the Saturday. He has had both halves of it since All Souls and never set them side by side. She sets them side by side, out here, in the wind, and goes on.

“She writes about her boys. And the raisins, and the rain. She says thank you for being a friend to her daughter for a weekend.” Lena doesn’t open the letter; she has it by heart. She says the next part slower. “And then she asks me something. *Do you remember what she was wearing? The police said a jean jacket. They never found it. Her grandmother made the patch.*”

There’s a photograph in the envelope. Lena opens her phone for the light, and the little screen comes up blue in the dark, and she holds the picture in it. Nora, on this wall, in daylight, sitting with her back to the camera and the sea in front of her, turned to look back over her shoulder at whoever was holding it, and laughing at them, her hair all over her face in the wind. She’s in a jean jacket. On the back of it, embroidered, Our Lady of Guadalupe: the gold rays around her, the roses at her feet. On the collar, small as a fingernail, a red Ferris wheel.
“I don’t know what she was wearing,” Lena says. “I was asleep.” Her hand goes to the medal at her throat.

He has held that jacket — in September, at ten past one in the morning, in his own room, it came up out of a black bag into his hands and unfolded, and Our Lady swung toward him with the stars on her mantle and the place where the thread was knotted, and somebody took it out of his hands — and the little red wheel he has seen too, this month, on a collar, through two inches of open zipper.

The wind comes up the bluff off the water, and the photograph shakes in her bare fingers in the blue light of the phone. “I’ve started it four times,” Lena says. “*Dear Mrs. Calloway.* And then I stop.”

journal.title: Nora Calloway
journal.text: The name on the plaque. Priya’s freshman roommate, Delgado 222. From Selma — raisins. Sang soprano; sang the Memorare in the shower. Philosophy. Fell at the Point at the end of April. September 8th would have been her twentieth birthday. Facebook won’t stop suggesting her. Her things are in a box in Priya’s room now. On the inside cover of her journal she promised whoever found it a song. All Souls: Lena wrote her name in the book. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. Julian wrote it too. Her mother wrote Lena for Christmas, care of Newman — the first Christmas; she says she’ll write every one. A picture of Nora on the wall at the Point, laughing. It was Lena’s weekend. The Saturday.

choices.key: At the Point Lena showed you a photograph her letter came with. You said nothing.
response: He reaches out and takes the corner of the photograph between his finger and thumb, so it won’t shake in the wind. She lets him. They hold it like that, a girl laughing on a wall, a corner each, until the screen of her phone dims and she has to press a key to bring Nora back, and then she puts her in the envelope, and the envelope in her coat.

choices.text: “Tell her mother you remember her laughing. That’s true.”
choices.key: At the Point Lena showed you a photograph her letter came with. You told her to tell Nora’s mother she remembers her laughing.
response: “Tell her mother you remember her laughing,” he says. “That’s true.”

Lena looks at the picture in the blue light, at the girl laughing, for as long as the screen stays lit. “That’s true,” she says. She puts the photograph back in the envelope, and the envelope in her coat, and keeps her hand on it there.

choices.key: At the Point Lena showed you a photograph her letter came with. You reached for your cigarettes, and she took one for the tin.
response: His hand goes into the Carhartt for the Marlboros and has the pack out and half open. She sees it in the light of the phone. She holds out her hand, and waits, and he puts the pack in it.

She shakes out one — only one — and gives him back the rest. The tin comes out of her coat pocket; the lid comes off; the cigarette goes in with the others, and the lid goes back on. “Not here,” she says, and the tin goes back in her coat with the letter. He doesn’t light anything.

s15a.slug: SATURDAY · 2:30 AM · THE POINT PATH → SEACLIFF ROAD
body: Going back is darker. They’re walking toward the houses now, and every house on Seacliff is dark, and the Lighthouse at the end of the fence is only a black block with the stars cut off square above it. The wind is behind them. She goes first again, fast, and at the gap in the fence she stops and waits for him, and when he comes through, her hand finds his.

Her bare hand, the one from the wall, cold all the way through, the glove still in her other fist. It finds his and takes hold, hard, and holds. Going past the back steps they wake the porch light, and it comes on behind them and throws the two of them out long across the lot to the side of the house, and clicks off again. At the curb, under the first streetlight on Seacliff, her hand lets go.
Two.

She puts the hand in her coat pocket, with the letter. For a mile there’s only their boots on the road and one dark rental after another with its blinds down and a couch on its roof, Las Olas gone home for Christmas; then the Grove, the eucalyptus dropping bark in the wind; and somewhere along the bike path she starts in on Laney’s fourteen coats, by color, in order of offense.

By the Lagoon the cold has gotten into them, the kind that comes up through the boots and stays. The bench is wet with it. The water lies black and flat and full of stars, and across it the Ferrer Tower stands up against the sky with no light anywhere in it.
“We could go up,” Jack says.
“Not tonight. They’d know it was us.” She looks along the dark halls on the water. “There’s nobody else.”

So she tells him Christmas instead, ahead of time, so he’ll have it. On Christmas Eve they drive up the River Road to St. James Parish after dark, Daddy’s truck and Luc’s car, Remy in the bed of the truck if Mama isn’t looking, and at seven o’clock they light the bonfires on the levee, one every half mile up the levee, cabins of logs and cane as tall as a house, so Papa Noël can find his way down the river in the dark. You can stand at one and see the next one burning, and the next. Then back down for Midnight Mass at Holy Rosary, and then Réveillon at two in the morning on Dupre Street: daube glacée, grillades and grits, oyster dressing, Mémère’s gumbo, bread pudding with whiskey sauce, and café brûlot that Daddy sets on fire in the good bowl every year while Mama tells him not by the curtains. He lets her get to the end of it.
“And Grandmère’s place,” she says. “Mama sets it. Every year since. We leave it empty.”

That’s all she says about it. He leaves it where she put it, and gives her Glenwood Avenue back: Nonna’s seven fishes on Christmas Eve — a light supper, she calls it — the baccalà soaking in the basement sink since Monday, smelts, calamari, shrimp, the clams, a white fish no one in the family has ever identified, and anchovies baked into the bread to make seven. Danny always called that cheating. His father in the short-term lot at Pittsburgh with the truck running since noon, because the heater takes a while and he doesn’t trust it.
“Call me Christmas Eve,” Lena says. “From the levee. I’ll hold the phone up so you can hear it burn.”
“I’ll call from the garage. It’s the only place nobody listens.”
“Fourteen you watch,” she says. “On the phone. From the garage. I don’t care what time it is in Ohio.” “I’ll watch.” She nods once, and that’s the end of Sully’s for the night.
She takes the card out of her coat and crosses off two lines on her knee, by feel, in the dark, and holds it up. Every line on it is gone.
“One more,” Jack says. “It’s not on your card.”

She looks at him, and puts the card away, and they go up the wet lawn to Delgado and in at the side door and up the east stairs past four floors of dark doors with the nameplates still on them, to the half-flight at the top.

s17.slug: SATURDAY · 4:00 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE ROOF
body: Up here the only light is the caged bulb over the roof door, and the stars. The popsicle stick is still in the strike, grayer than it was in September, and the door still promises an alarm it has no intention of keeping.

Gravel under their boots; the elevator housing; the parapet at the hip. The Lagoon lies flat one way with the stars in it, and the hills lie black the other way, and out on the grass below there’s one square of light from the whole building: Priya’s window, still up. It’s four o’clock in the morning, three nights before the longest night of the year, and the van comes at a quarter to five.

Lena walks the roof once, around the parapet, with her hands in her coat, looking at everything, and stops on the west side, where past the black of the Grove you can just make out the Point against the stars, the place they were two hours ago. Out over the water a late one from Monday draws a short line and is gone.
“Forty-five,” she says. “Costigan, one.”
“Margot’s going to want that in writing.”

“Margot’s in Portland. She can come and get it.” She puts her chin down into her scarf. “Last time I was up here at night, she and I went at each other till three. Both of us crying. Neither one of us gave an inch.” A minute. “She lit him a candle today.”
“For research.”
“For research.” Lena looks down at the gravel. “I’m going to miss her. If you tell her I said so, I’ll deny it in Latin.”
“Whose Latin?”
“Augustine’s. She can’t stand him. It’ll be twice the insult.”
She comes back along the parapet to where he is. “What’s the first thing you do?” he says. “When you get in.”

“Sleep. In my own bed, with Josie in it by two, because she’ll come in and say she had a dream. She’s thirteen. She hasn’t had a dream since she was nine; she has an agenda.” Lena turns and puts her back to the parapet. “Then Mama takes my temperature without asking, and Daddy feeds me boudin in the truck before we’re out of the airport, and Mémère looks at me and says something in French that means I’m thin.”
“Nonna’ll say it in Italian. To my mother. About me. In front of me.”
“They should meet.”
“They’d unionize.”

“Lord. They’d organize the Gulf.” She laughs down into her scarf, and the laugh goes, and she turns around again to face the hills, where there isn’t any light yet and won’t be for hours. Her breath smokes in the cold. The scarf has come loose at one side, and her hair is coming out of it, and the bulb over the door puts a little light along the edge of her jaw and nowhere else, and her nose is red, and she is looking at the hills as though she means to remember them for a test.

He has been carrying it since the porch light went off, and before that since August, since a pelican lamp in a parking lot, and it has gotten heavier at every line she crossed off. Up here, with the van coming and nothing left on her card and the building asleep under their boots but for one light, it comes up out of his chest into his mouth all at once — the thing they don’t say on Glenwood Avenue, where they say *text me when you get there* and then don’t sleep — and he turns to her at the parapet.
She sees him turn.

choices.text: “Lena. I have to tell you something, and I don’t get to.”
choices.key: On the roof, three nights before the longest night, you told Lena you had something to tell her and didn’t get to.
response: “Lena. I have to tell you something, and I don’t get to.”
“Then don’t,” she says, quickly, before the next word can get out. “Not on a roof. Not with a van coming.” Her voice is what stops him; her hands stay in her coat, and her eyes stay on him.
So he doesn’t. It stays out on the cold air in front of them, the thing he didn’t get to, close enough to put a hand on, and neither of them puts a hand on it.

choices.key: On the roof, three nights before the longest night, you started to say it, and stopped yourself.
response: “I’m in —”
He hears where it’s going and stops it himself.

“Jack,” she says. Only his name, with the warning in it and the asking in it both, and her eyes on his face. He lets the rest of it stay unfinished, out in the cold, and it doesn’t go anywhere. She breathes out, long and white in the light from the door, and puts her chin back down into her scarf, and watches him over the top of it.

choices.text: “This was the best night I’ve had since —”
choices.key: On the roof you told Lena it was the best night you’d had since — and neither of you finished.
response: “This was the best night I’ve had since —”
“Since?”
“Since ever.”

“Don’t,” she says, gently. “Not while I’m —” and she doesn’t finish hers either. She shakes her head at the hills, once, and laughs a little at the both of them, and they leave both halves of it out on the parapet in the cold.

choices.text: “I’d say something, but you’d grade it.”
choices.key: On the roof you told Lena you’d say something, but she’d grade it.
response: “I’d say something, but you’d grade it.”

“I’d give it an A,” Lena says. She looks at him a long time in the light from the door. “That’s the problem.” It starts out a joke and comes out of her true, and she hears it, and laughs at herself in the cold, once, and leaves it standing.

choices.key: On the roof you didn’t say it. You looked at her.
response: He looks at her instead, with the caged bulb behind her and the cold between his teeth, and lets her see the night on his face, and keeps his mouth shut on the rest.
She sees it all on him. She stands there in it with her hands in her coat, and when she can, very quietly, she says, “Thank you.”

s17a.slug: SATURDAY · 4:15 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE ROOF
body: When the cold has had long enough at both of them, Lena takes the 8-Ball out of her coat pocket. She shuts her eyes and asks it something with her lips still, and shakes it once, hard, and carries it over to the roof door to read it under the caged bulb. It surprises a laugh out of her, short and bright, up into the cold, and she comes back and holds the little window up for him.
*ASK AGAIN LATER.*
“Your saint’s a diplomat.”
“Shake it again.” “You don’t shake it again. That’s how you break them.” She turns it over in her glove so the little window faces her palm.
She puts it away.
At the roof door she stops with her hand on the bar, the bulb right over her, the light in her hair and the dark of the stairwell in front of her, and turns her head halfway back. “Jack —”
He waits.
“Bring the coffee back empty.”

And she goes down the stairs ahead of him. He gives the roof a last look — the gravel, the parapet, the one square of light on the grass — and follows her, past the popsicle stick, and behind him the alarm doesn’t sound. It hasn’t in a decade.

journal.title: The roof
journal.text: Fifth floor: EMERGENCY EXIT ONLY · ALARM WILL SOUND, and under it, in Sharpie gone brown: (it won’t). It doesn’t. A popsicle stick in the strike. Tar, gravel, the elevator housing, a parapet to the hip. The Lagoon one way, the hills the other. The last night, three nights before the longest one: the last stop.

s18.slug: SATURDAY · 4:40 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE LOBBY → THE 101 SOUTH
body: At twenty to five every light in the Delgado lobby is on and there’s no one in it to use them: the fluorescents over the mail cubbies, the lamp on the front desk, the exit signs, the urn unplugged with a strip of masking tape across its spigot. Out past the glass doors the front circle is still black. Lena is standing by the desk with her suitcase upright at her knee and her coat buttoned to the chin. Jack comes down the east stairs with the duffel on his shoulder and Theo’s throw rolled tight under the strap.

body.text: The RAZR is in the inside pocket of the Carhartt, still off. He took it off the bare desk with the duffel on his way out, and left 412 with nothing in it but Theo’s espresso machine.

body: The office door behind the desk opens, and Priya comes out in a plaid flannel robe and her retainer, with the clipboard against her chest and a headlamp strapped on over her hair and switched on, in a lobby where every light is burning. She has a pen.
“Broussard.”
“Present.”
“Costigan.”
The pen waits over the clipboard.
“Present,” Jack says.

Priya looks at him over the clipboard with the headlamp putting a white circle on his chest. “Write it down, somebody,” she says, and when no one does she does it herself, a check mark pressed into the paper hard enough to hear.

She holds out a manila envelope with 217 and 412 on it in marker. Their keys go in. She licks the flap and seals it with the side of her fist, and takes a card each for them off a stack on the desk, still warm from the laminator.

body.title: A laminated card, from a stack on the front desk
body.text:
SAFE TRAVELS.
THIS IS NOT A REQUEST.
— Priya, RA

body: “You laminated goodbye,” Lena says.
“I laminated an instruction.” Priya clicks the headlamp off. “The van has been outside for two minutes. Get in it.”
Lena puts her arms around her, robe and clipboard and all, and Priya stands it with the clipboard held out to one side and says over Lena’s shoulder, to Jack, “January. Both of you. On my lawn.”

The van is a white fifteen-seater idling at the curb with a magnetic sign on the door, a phone number and a cartoon airplane, and the driver, a big quiet man in a Dodgers cap and gloves with the fingers cut off, puts her suitcase and his duffel in the back without asking whose is whose. They’re the only pickup. They take the back bench.

He takes them out Ocean Road and onto the 101 south in the dark, with the heater on high and an oldies station low on the radio. Up in the hills, where the road climbs away from the coast, the station gives them Simon and Garfunkel — the long slow one about two kids on a bus going east, the guitar walking along under it. They don’t talk. Lena watches the dark go by on her side with her hands in her coat pockets. At Gaviota the road comes down out of the pass to the sea and turns and runs along it, the railroad between the highway and the water and the Channel black past that, with a few lights out on it too far off to name.
Somewhere past Gaviota her head comes down on his shoulder.
Three.

Her hair is against his jaw. Her breathing is slow and even and tells him nothing — asleep or not, he can’t tell — and he doesn’t move. The song ends, and the station goes on to something else and then to a man selling mattresses, and he keeps his shoulder where it is past Refugio and El Capitán and the dark campgrounds, with the driver’s eyes coming up in the mirror now and then and going back to the road, and her weight on him, and the heater going, and thirty miles of coast going by in the dark on the right-hand side.

journal.title: Priya (RA)
journal.text: Laminates things. Owns an air horn. Her freshman roommate was Nora Calloway. The one rule she doesn’t laminate is for her. Three jobs: RA, the library overnight desk, orgo tutor. Failing orgo, she says. Her parents run a motel in Fremont and think she’s going to be a doctor. Re-laminated the laundry room at two in the morning, on her twenty-first birthday. Her mother’s text came in at the dryers. She didn’t answer it in front of me. Alarm Five: the only name on four she couldn’t check was mine. ‘Costigan. You were not on my lawn.’ Sunday at four in the morning she found a card on her door. ‘Unbelievable.’ The last roll, 4:40 a.m., in a headlamp: Costigan — present.

body: The Santa Barbara airport is a white Spanish house with a red tile roof and a lamp over every door, and at a quarter to six it’s lit up and only half awake: a man running a floor polisher in slow loops past the gift shop, a coffee cart with its shutter up, the departures on a TV bolted high on the wall. Lena’s airline has its counter open. His has a sign on a stand: OPENS 6:00 AM. She checks her suitcase and comes back with her boarding pass folded into her missal.

At the coffee cart she’s humming. It’s so low he only hears it standing next to her: one note, held, under the polisher and the PA and everything else. He buys a muffin. They sit at the cart’s one little table.

body.text: There are no beignets. There’s a blueberry muffin the size of a fist, in plastic. She eats half and gives him the other half.
“Julian told you to make me eat,” she says. “He did.” “He would.” She eats half and gives him the other half.
He puts the muffin in front of her and doesn’t say who asked. She eats half and gives him the other half.

body: When it’s gone she sweeps the crumbs off the table into her palm and into the napkin, and her hand goes into her coat and comes out with the Altoids tin, RELIQUARY on the lid. She sets it on the table and pushes it across to him with one finger.
“Keep it over Christmas,” she says. “Count them. If there’s one missing in January, I’ll know.” Her finger stays on the lid. “If there’s one more, I’ll know that too.”

body.text: “Eleven, now.”

body: He puts it in the pocket of the Carhartt, where it rides against his hip with its small weight. The Benedict holy card is in his shirt pocket, where he moved it Wednesday for the oral and has been moving it shirt to shirt since. He takes it out and lays it on the table where the tin was: the Pope in white and red with one hand up, a little blurred in the printing, the corners soft from a semester of back pockets.
“Be nice to him.”
Lena picks it up and looks at Benedict, and Benedict looks back at her, mild and a little shy in his red cape.
“I’m always nice to him,” she says. “I just don’t *swoon*.”
She laughs first, and he does, at the little table, with the floor polisher going by. She puts the Pope in the missal at a ribbon and shuts it on him.
The line for the checkpoint is a dozen people between two blue ropes, moving. He walks her to the mouth of it, and there she turns around and puts her arms around him.

He holds on. Her cheek is against his collar and her hair is under his chin, and through two coats he can feel her breathing. Ahead of her the line goes through the podium one at a time until there’s no one left in front of her. The man behind her, a businessman with a garment bag, moves the bag from one hand to the other, and reads the departures on the TV, and moves it back.
Into his collar, small, she says, “Tell Nonna Mémère’s still lighting the whole name.”
“I’ll tell her.”

He doesn’t let go, and she doesn’t. At the podium the agent says, “Next.” And again, “Next,” and this time it’s her, and they come apart, and she goes in between the ropes with her license and her pass held out.

He stands at the rope and watches her through it. The agent reads her license and looks at her and at it, and makes a mark. She puts her coat in one gray bin and her bag in another and pushes them onto the rollers, and walks through the arch with her hands at her sides.

On the far side the belt stops. The screener says something to the man beside him, and the man reaches into the bin with her coat and comes up with the 8-Ball. He holds it to the light. He gives it a good shake, turns it over and reads it, and looks at Lena over the top of it. “Outlook good,” he tells her, loud enough for the rope, and gives it back.

She puts her coat on. At the corner where the hall turns toward the gates she stops, and turns around, and finds him at the rope, and says something, short. The PA picks that moment to remind everybody about unattended bags, and the belt starts up again, and he gets nothing of it but the shape of her mouth, which is the wrong shape for *Merry Christmas*. She laughs at whatever his face is doing, and lifts her hand, and goes around the corner.

At six the man at his airline’s counter takes the sign off its stand. Jack checks the duffel through to Pittsburgh and goes through the same checkpoint with the same agent, who reads his license and waves him on. The RAZR rides the belt by itself in a gray bin, shut and dark.

Out the holdroom window the apron is lit white under its lamps, and over the mountains the sky has gone from black to a deep gray-blue. Her plane is the little jet nearest the glass, the airstairs folded up into it and the door shut, and a man in ear protectors walking backward in front of it with two orange wands. At 6:31 it starts to roll.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear.

journal.title: The Reliquary
journal.text: An Altoids tin from a pea-soup restaurant in Buellton. RELIQUARY on the lid. No. 1: the Lighthouse. No. 2: Malibu, before breakfast. No. 3: the harbor — she smoked half of it first. No. 4: a clove, on the Delgado roof, at a wake. By dispensation. Do not ask. No. 5: the Ferrer Tower, in the bells. No. 6: Lucia, a motel porch, under the stars — on the back of the receipt. No. 7: Del Playa, on the widow’s walk, on the back of a HALO OR HORNS card. All Hallows — the occasion. No. 8: the east stairs, before light, the morning after All Souls. She smoked half. On the back of an All Souls card — she wrote All Souls anyway. No. 9: Campus Point, Veterans Day, on the back of the 12:10 worship aid. No. 10: the Walgreens on Mission Street, St. Nicholas Eve, half past one in the morning, out of my own pocket. ‘For the saint.’ Into her cardigan. She’ll file it. No. 11: the Point, the last night. She took it before I could light it. ‘Not here.’ She gave me the tin to keep over Christmas. Count them.

choices.key: At the SBA window you said Father Osei’s blessing again, for her plane.
response: He says it under his breath at the glass, and changes *them* to *her* as he goes: a help when she sets out, and a comfort on the road. A shade in the heat. A cover in the rain and in the cold. A staff where the way is slippery, and a harbor. The little jet turns at the end of the runway and comes back past the window the other way at full throttle, and lifts, and banks away south over the water. He crosses himself with the hand that isn’t holding his boarding pass.
At ten past seven his own flight takes off, and the first sun is on the Santa Ynez as the wheels leave the ground.

choices.text: Watch it until there’s nothing to watch.
choices.key: At the SBA window you watched her plane until there was nothing to watch.
response: He watches it go down to the far end of the runway and turn and hold there with its lights going. Then it comes, and lifts off over the slough, and climbs, and banks out over the water with the gray going light behind it: a jet, and then a shape, and then a light on a wing, and then a place in the sky he keeps looking at after there’s nothing in it.
At ten past seven his own flight takes off, and the first sun is on the Santa Ynez as the wheels leave the ground.

choices.key: At the SBA window you opened the tin and counted them.
response: He takes the tin out of the Carhartt and opens it on the sill. They’re all there, the cigarettes and the scraps she filed them on — a receipt, a party card, a worship aid — packed in tight so they won’t roll.
He closes it. Out on the apron the little jet is rolling, and by the time he looks up it’s in the air.
At ten past seven his own flight takes off, and the first sun is on the Santa Ynez as the wheels leave the ground.

s20.slug: SATURDAY · 11:05 AM MST · DENVER INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT, CONCOURSE B
body: The light in Denver is a different light: high and hard and blue, coming in off the plains through the window at the far end of Concourse B, where he has an hour and twenty minutes before Pittsburgh. Past the parked jets the ground runs flat and brown to the west and stops at the mountains, and the mountains are white, the Front Range laid along the bottom of the sky with snow on every one of them.
Jack takes the RAZR out of his jacket and holds the red key down.
It plays its four notes going back up the stairs, and the screen comes on white and hunts. *Searching.* It finds Denver. It buzzes in his hand, and buzzes again. *2 New Messages.*

body.text: Fourteen and oh tonight. It’s ordained. Merry Christmas, Youngstown. —L.

body: He reads it standing at the glass with his other hand in the pocket of the Carhartt, around the tin.

body.text: *Picture Msg* · so you have something to look forward to in january...

body: He opens it.

A gray box comes up on the little screen that says *Retrieving*, with a bar under it that fills from the left, slowly. At the end the picture arrives all at once, too bright, the concourse’s overhead lights laid across the screen in a white sheet. He turns his back on them and shades the phone in the cup of his hand, and the picture comes up out of the glare.

A full-length mirror on the back of a bedroom door. The room is in it behind her: a twin bed with a white quilt pulled up square, and over the bed a corkboard crowded with old call sheets pinned on top of one another, curling at the corners. It’s early wherever it is. The light comes from a window he can’t see, gray going gold, and it reaches one side of her and not the other.

She has nothing on but the braided anklet. She is standing square to the glass, one hip a little out, all of her in that early light, and this time she has taken the trouble: the white phone is held up level in front of her face, steady, both elbows in, so that it covers one eye and the camera’s own small eye looks out where hers would be.
The half of her face the phone doesn’t hide is level and patient, almost serious, the mouth closed. The one eye is on the lens and nowhere else.
He stands at the window in Denver with it in the cup of his hand, and the snow on the mountains behind it.
